item.title: Nvidia C.E.O. Scandal Sets Off a Blitz of A.I. Memes
item.description:
Jensen Huang and his leather-clad likeness had become synonymous with the technological giant he co-founded, Nvidia. They were so entwined that, this year, the company sold $178 sweaters with a pixel-art version of Mr. Huang on the front.

Now, in the wake of Mr. Huang’s resignation on Thursday after back-to-back cheating scandals, including an extramarital affair with a woman the U.S. government believes is a Chinese spy, the internet has taken ahold of his image to unleash a flood of memes.

In many cases, they are being made by A.I. enthusiasts who revered Mr. Huang.

Images of Mr. Huang have appeared in online parodies of music videos, Bollywood movies, American sitcoms and kiss-cams at Coldplay concerts — many generated using artificial intelligence, the technology that became widely available through the chips Nvidia produces.

The revelations about Mr. Huang, 63, one of the most powerful figures in the A.I. boom, are part of a long list of infidelity scandals that became memes.

Last year, the married chief executive of a tech start-up was caught on a kiss-cam at a Coldplay concert embracing the married but separated head of his company’s human resources department.

Mr. Huang’s image was superimposed on that viral moment by Peter Dedene, a Belgian software engineer. He said in a phone interview on Thursday that he was up late this week on his phone, scrolling the headlines about Nvidia.

Without leaving his bed, Mr. Dedene, 43, used an open-source generative A.I. tool to substitute the couple from the Coldplay concert with images of Mr. Huang and Alice Huang, the Chinese businesswoman with whom Mr. Huang has admitted having an affair.

“I didn’t think a lot of it,” Mr. Dedene said of his meme.

When he woke up on Sunday morning, he said, the post had over a million impressions. As of Thursday afternoon, it had nearly seven million.

“I really looked up to this guy,” Mr. Dedene said of Mr. Huang, adding, “It’s sort of hilarious that, in the end, the technology he cocreated is now enabling these kinds of jokes.”

Social media users have used A.I. to place Mr. Huang in iconic music videos about cheating.

In one post, Mr. Huang, donning his signature black leather jacket, takes Usher’s place in his music video for “Confessions, Pt. II.” (The lip-syncing is better in the original version.)

Thomas Unise, an A.I. consultant in Minneapolis who made the video, said it took him five minutes to find four images of Mr. Huang on Google and feed them into an A.I. tool to substitute Mr. Huang’s image for Usher’s in the video.

Mr. Unise, 40, said the proliferation of memes using Mr. Huang’s image illustrated how rapidly the technology had advanced.

“A year and a half ago, Will Smith eating spaghetti looked like a bunch of smears all over the screen,” he said of the actor and musician. “You can watch a video now and be like, ‘Wow, this actually looks pretty dang real.’”

In another video, Mr. Huang plays the character Neo in a scene from the movie “The Matrix.” President Trump, as the character Morpheus, lectures him on the importance of maintaining strategic competition with China and not falling for the woman in the red dress.

Mr. Huang’s avatar turns around to realize that the woman, replaced with an image of Ms. Huang, has become Xi Jinping, the Chinese leader, brandishing a gun.

Elon Musk also makes a cameo in the meme, which as of Thursday had more than six million views on X.

On the theme of high-stakes deceit in Silicon Valley, some users placed Mr. Huang into “You Can See Everything,” the documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, the Theranos founder who went to prison for defrauding investors.

With the help of generative A.I., users recast a montage from the documentary’s trailer in which Ms. Huang — as Ms. Holmes — unblinkingly insists, “Of course I’m not deceiving you.”

Many of the videos have labels identifying them as artificially generated.

But it’s “still surprising,” Mr. Dedene said of his video, how many people asked: “‘Is this real?’”

Ephrat Livni contributed reporting.

item.title: Paul Barril, French ‘Supergendarme’ Turned Mercenary, Has Died
item.description:
Paul Barril’s offer to African dictators was straightforward: Your opponents will be subjected to surveillance and manipulation. Newspapers will be “infiltrated.” Plots against the state will be “neutralized.”

Plenty of heads of state took up the services he offered, including Omar Bongo in Gabon and Denis Sassou-Nguesso in Congo. Other clients went to Paris to do their shopping at his Security Action Store, which offered the latest in bulletproof vests or night-vision goggles, as Mr. Barril recounted in one of his six autobiographies, “The Elysee’s Secret Wars” (1996).

Mr. Barril was often described in the news media as a former French “supergendarme” for his longtime work in elite units. After he left the gendarmerie, or national police, in 1984, he became a security adviser and mercenary provider across the African continent and was implicated by human rights groups in the Rwandan genocide of 1994.

His death, on Oct. 20 at 80 at his home in Antibes, France, was announced by the French interior ministry. He had Parkinson’s disease.

By the time he founded his mercenary-security company, Secrets, a French acronym for Security Equipment Planning and Realization Company, in 1984, Mr. Barril was a well-chronicled public figure.

In the gendarmerie, which in France is under the military, he joined a new military police intervention unit, the GIGN, in 1974. The French news media chronicled Mr. Barril’s reputation as an ultrafit top cop, a military-grade swimmer and diver, a black belt in karate, a parachutist, a hostage liberator and a policeman working inside and outside the law. With the GIGN, he participated in the 1979 operation against Islamist militants who had seized the Grand Mosque in Mecca, taking dozens hostage.

In 1982, he became part of President François Mitterrand’s special antiterrorism police unit. That year, Mr. Barril was implicated in a murky affair in which he was alleged to have having planted weapons and explosives in the apartment of Irish nationalists in Vincennes, near Paris. French judicial authorities dropped the court case in 2002 on legal technicalities.

“We did the operation. We prevented bloodshed. I don’t acknowledge anything, ever,” Mr. Barril said on the French television program “Tout Le Monde En Parle” in 2000. “I would do the same thing all over again.”

It was in Africa that Mr. Barril gained the reputation that was to keep him at the center of French newspaper investigations, judicial probes and human-rights group complaints for decades.

With another former colleague from the gendarmerie, Mr. Barril was “at the service of the principal despotic governments of Africa and the Middle East, under the forgiving eye of the French security services,” according to the 2021 book “The Empire That Won’t Die: A History of Françafrique,” written by a collective of historians, journalists and human rights activists.

The book called Mr. Barril and his former colleague “emblematic figures” of “Françafrique,” a term employed in France and Africa to designate the murky official and unofficial networks — military, financial and political — entangling France with its former colonies. In 1990, Mr. Barril, for instance, recruited 15 mercenaries to teach the police in Gabon how to use tear gas against demonstrators, according to the book.

His connections with the Hutu government of Rwanda, responsible for the 1994 genocide in which close to one million Tutsis were murdered, earned him his greatest scrutiny.

In 2013, the Human Rights League of France, Survie, a human rights organization, and the International Federation for Human Rights accused him of “complicity in genocide” for supplying weapons and training to the Hutus. French magistrates investigated Mr. Barril’s role in Rwanda for years but never charged him.

Mr. Barril didn’t deny being in Rwanda at the time of the genocide. During a search of the Paris offices of his company, the French authorities found a May 1994 contract signed by Mr. Barril and the Rwandan prime minister in which Mr. Barril committed to supplying the Hutu government with “20 men for training purposes,” “two million cartridges” of varying calibers, “shells and mortars” and “grenades.”

The contract, which noted a fee of $3.13 million, was a violation of the United Nations arms embargo on Rwanda, and it was evidence that his men were helping the killers.

In June 1994, the Rwandan government paid him $1.2 million of the sum, according to Human Rights Watch; but before the contract could be fully carried out, Paul Kagame, who led a Tutsi-dominated rebel group and later became president, entered Kigali, the capital, on July 4, 1994, and halted the killing by the Hutus.

“There were three million dead” during the Rwandan civil war, Mr. Barril said on a television program six years later. “It’s the greatest historical lie ever. They’ve put it over that one ethnic group massacred another, when really, it was the opposite.”

Mr. Barril always hinted to investigators that he had been acting under the indirect direction of President Mitterrand’s administration, which had been allied with Rwanda’s Hutu government.

But his former boss in the GIGN, Christian Prouteau, said in an interview that Mr. Barril’s claims were nonsense.

“He had no mission, despite what he pretended subsequently,” Mr. Prouteau said. “As soon as he left the gendarmerie, at no moment whatsoever did he have a mandate from France.”

“He passed from the light to the darkness,” Mr. Prouteau added.

Paul Barril, the son and grandson of gendarmes, was born on April 13, 1946, in Vinay, in the Vercors region in southeastern France. He spent his childhood in the high Alps, the area where his father was posted.

At 18, Mr. Barril joined the army, was assigned to a tank unit in West Berlin, then returned to France for training at the gendarme sub-officers’ school, emerging top of his class. He went back to West Berlin, where one of his missions was to guard Rudolf Hess, the last remaining Nazi war criminal at Spandau Prison.

Mr. Barril took pity on the old man and, in the first of his memoirs, “Missions Très Spéciales” (1984), fantasized about liberating him. In 1975, he graduated from the gendarmes officer-training school in Melun, France, again at the top of his class.

Not long after Mr. Prouteau helped organize the GIGN in the 1970s, Mr. Barril presented himself in his office, and he became the older officer’s second in command. “He was a flamboyant young officer, brilliant and courageous,” Mr. Prouteau recalled. “He made some dangerous arrests, without arms.”

Things turned sour with the scandal over the arrest of the Irish militants. Twenty years later, Mr. Barril was caught up in another state scandal dating from those years: He received a six-month suspended sentence in 2005 and a fine for having been part of an illegal wiretapping ring in which dozens of politicians, actors, journalists, union leaders and others were bugged during the Mitterrand years.

“You’re not necessarily bugging people to hurt them,” Mr. Barril said on the 2000 television program.

In the meantime, according to Mr. Prouteau, Mr. Barril had gained a considerable fortune working for the emir of Qatar, among others, until illness overtook him at the beginning of the 2010s.

Mr. Barril is survived by his wife, Angélique, and his son, Patrick.

“He always had a nasty relationship with money,” Mr. Prouteau recalled. “And he was fascinated by mercenaries.”

After Mr. Prouteau was shot during a 1980 GIGN operation, he added: “Paul was in the hospital every day. Then, he became the other Barril. I can’t accept that.”

Daphné Anglès contributed research.

item.title: Microsoft’s Global Outage and Fixes: What We Know
item.description:
Microsoft is reporting widespread improvements to its services after a global outage took them offline on Thursday, disrupting communications and work at schools, government agencies and offices around the world. The company, headquartered in Redmond, Wash., said on Friday that it was seeing “encouraging recovery progress, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across a growing portion of affected infrastructure.”

“We remain focused on addressing residual impact and ensuring reliable service restoration,” the company added.

Here’s what to know as of Friday afternoon.

Outages started disrupting Microsoft tools and apps around noon Eastern time on Thursday and quickly spread to more than 70 countries and territories, affecting millions of users, according to Downdetector, an outage-tracking site.

Some of Microsoft’s most popular products, including the email manager Outlook, the workplace messaging and video calling app Teams and the artificial intelligence assistant Copilot, stopped working.

Microsoft said in a statement on Friday that “for now, we can confirm that there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity.” It added that the problem was “a technical issue not related to cyber or A.I.” agents.

The company has yet to provide a clear answer, although it has promised to make public a full report that identifies the “root cause” of the outage.

In statements on Thursday and Friday, it provided some details.

Microsoft said on Thursday that “a portion of infrastructure” was experiencing “elevated load across multiple regions, which is likely contributing to the connectivity errors.” That could mean that increased stress on its network was caused by a “number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable, straining the remaining infrastructure,” the company said.

Microsoft said the servers were failing health checks — periodic, automated assessments that ensure they are functioning correctly and efficiently. It said the failed health checks “may originate from a specific component that’s responsible for processing server health.”

On Friday, Microsoft said the problem had been introduced to the system “during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change.” It said it had addressed the underlying issue, allowing its tools and apps to begin to function normally again.

“Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage,” it said. “While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration.”

Luca Arnaboldi, an assistant professor of cybersecurity at the School of Computer Science at the University of Birmingham in England, said the outage was a reminder that when people use “the cloud,” they are actually relying on servers, which have finite resources.

“In this particular case, as servers became unavailable, capacity on the remaining servers increased, leaving fewer machines to handle the traffic,” he said in a statement. Even after some of the original servers came back online, he added, “the ones currently under strain now fail, creating a constant catch-up.”

Parents struggled to contact their children’s schools, some government services faltered and many office workers could not access email.

The outage affected parts of the federal government, including the U.S. House of Representatives, according to Samantha Carter, a spokeswoman for the office that oversees House operations.

“We have seen improvements to Outlook’s functionality this morning, but will continue to monitor the situation until all issues are resolved and full functionality is restored to all Microsoft applications,” Ms. Carter said in an email on Friday.

Elsewhere in the world, Britain’s National Health Service said the outage was having a “disruptive impact.” The National Pharmacy Association of Britain said the issues at the N.H.S. were making it difficult for pharmacies to communicate with doctors and some patients, which could cause delays in filling prescriptions. The Metropolitan Police in London said its online contact forms weren’t working.

In Australia, intelligence and police forces said that their operations had been affected. Singapore told taxpayers that email had been disrupted, and the Supreme Court of the Philippines and the European Court of Human Rights said the outage could cause delays in its work.

Reporting was contributed by Isabella Kwai, Karla Adam and Adeel Hassan.

item.title: Timing of Climate Science Reports Ignites a Hot Fight at U.N. Talks
item.description:
A squabble over the publication timetable for several climate reports has turned into one of the burning issues of this year’s United Nations climate conference, as some warn that fossil fuel interests might be interfering with the world’s pre-eminent climate science organization.

The U.N.-backed Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change produces landmark reports that generally come out every five to seven years. The next round of reports would take on topics like physical changes to the earth and greenhouse gas emissions.

Timing is critical because in 2028 nations are supposed to assess their progress and then ramp up their efforts to do more, based on the best science. That process, known as a stocktake and occurring every five years, is the engine of the Paris Agreement.

Saudi Arabia, India and Russia are among those pushing to delay the reports so that at least two of them come out after 2028.

The fact that those nations rank among the largest fossil fuel exporters or importers has led to accusations that coal, oil and gas interests might be interfering with science.

“Saudi Arabia is trying to destroy the I.P.C.C. in order to prevent the next global stocktake from using the accurate scientific data on fossil fuels,” said former Vice President Al Gore, who is in Turkey for the talks.

At COP31, the United Nations climate talks being held this year in Antalya, Turkey, a handful of world leaders warned that the United Nations’ climate science body is being undermined.

“I am deeply troubled” by the impasse, said Prime Minister Feleti Teo, of Tuvalu, whose island nation lies barely six feet above sea level. “Our survival demands collective actions to be guided by science and not by politics.”

Many small developing nations, as well as the European Union, want all three I.P.C.C. reports to come before this next assessment period so the science can inform new policies. The United Nations secretary general, António Guterres, said on Friday that he, too, was in favor of that timetable.

But that group is facing big pushback.

The nations that have sought a delay, which also include China and Kenya, have said they want to ease pressure on government reviewers, according to meeting accounts from the International Institute for Sustainable Development, an independent research organization. Smaller countries without resources have a harder time managing this workload, they say, and faster turnaround time could compromise scientific rigor.

Representatives from Russia, Saudi Arabia, India, China and Iran did not respond to a request for comment.

Patricia Nying’uro, a meteorologist who is Kenya’s lead representative to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, said that Kenya’s position “comes down to capacity, not politics.”

In 2023, countries agreed to transition away from coal, oil and gas. It was the only time a United Nations climate agreement has explicitly referenced fossil fuels.

This year, the Trump administration announced it was withdrawing from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change and dozens of other international organizations and treaties, calling them “contrary to the interests” of the United States.

One I.P.C.C. negotiator, who requested anonymity because he was not authorized to speak publicly, said that in previous years the United States had been a “mediating influence” in talks, one that hasn’t been replaced. In 2013, for instance, Saudi Arabia contested the key findings of a panel’s report but then backed off.

The impasse has complicated the talks in Antalya, which began on Monday.

Diana Acconcia, a senior European Commission climate official, said Friday that if the I.P.C.C. issue were not resolved, it might not be possible for the representatives from 190 countries that have gathered in Turkey to agree on other matters.

“It is not separable from the COP discussions here,” Ms. Acconcia said, adding, “Europe stands on the side of science.”

The climate talks are scheduled to run until Nov. 20.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, established in 1988, assesses available climate science but does not conduct its own research. It depends on scientists who volunteer to scrutinize existing studies, synthesize findings and draft reports that often span more than 1,000 pages. As part of the timeline fight, its upcoming budget has also been left in limbo.

“Our authors deserve clarity and certainty,” said Jim Skea, a British scientist who chairs the I.P.C.C. “I encourage member governments to spare no effort to find consensus and reach a decision.”

item.title: U.S. Visa Restrictions Threaten African Contestants in Miss Universe
item.description:
At least two African contestants for Miss Universe said they were in danger of missing the pageant in Puerto Rico this month because they had not secured U.S. visas amid a crackdown by the Trump administration.

One contestant, Miss Zambia, Mubanga Pamela Hatyoka, said she would not travel to the annual event on Nov. 24 because she had not received her visa, according to Arm Model Management, which said it was the franchise holder of Miss Zambia 2026.

Her nonattendance is “linked to the United States presidential travel restrictions affecting Zambia and other African nations,” the agency said in a statement on social media. “She earned her crown, she earned her title, and she deserves the opportunity to represent the nation she proudly serves.”

The contestant from Zimbabwe, Roseanna Hall, said on social media that she, too, had not received a U.S. visa. “I will not give up,” she said. Contestants from South Sudan and the Republic of Congo also faced delays, according to news reports.

The Miss Universe organization did not immediately reply to a request for comment. The Department of Homeland Security also did not respond to a similar request. It was unclear why the contestants had not received visas.

The social media page of the Miss Universe organization listed 20 African countries among its contestants for the pageant to held in the U.S. territory.

The Trump administration has curtailed several avenues to legal migration to the United States as part of a crackdown, including visa bans and restrictions that have hit African countries hard. The administration in January imposed full or partial travel bans and visa restrictions on 36 countries, and 29 of those are in Africa.

In December, the Trump administration widened travel restrictions to additional countries, including Zambia and Zimbabwe, while keeping in place full restrictions for citizens of the Republic of Congo and adding them for South Sudan.

Homeland Security has said it was “slamming the door shut on the foreign invaders who have undermined our national security.”

Citizens of African countries have for decades complained of draconian visa rules imposed by the governments of the United States and European countries. Governments say the restrictions aim to control migration and prevent fraud, but many Africans say they impede legitimate professional, business and study opportunities and stop family members from attending occasions such as births, weddings and funerals.

Those restrictions have become more severe since public attitudes in many Western countries have turned against immigration over the past decade.

item.title: Here’s the latest.
item.description:
The Federal Aviation Administration announced a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday afternoon, in what appeared to be a major outage affecting its air traffic control system.

Markwayne Mullin, the secretary of homeland security, blamed the ground stop on a telecommunication outage but said Trump administration officials did not know the cause, adding that it would take an extended period of time to fix the issues. “This isn’t going to just be resolved and turned around within the hour,” he said. “This is going to take some time.”

Sean Duffy, the secretary of transportation, confirmed the outage in a social media post, citing “a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.”

“FAA technicians are investigating the issue,” he added. “We will provide immediate updates as we have them.”

The agency posted an advisory stating that “all airports are ground stopped,” citing “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety” as the reasons.

“All departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice,” the official advisory read, adding that the landings of inbound international flights would be managed on a case-by-case basis.

Shortly after the advisory was posted, an F.A.A. website that lists air traffic control system notices appeared to have gone down, erasing dozens of notices that previously had been listed.

The stoppage, which began shortly before 4 p.m., could affect hundreds of flights already airborne, in addition to airplanes on the ground waiting to take off. As of about 4:45 p.m., there were more than 7,800 flights delayed in the United States and about 350 cancellations, according to FlightAware, a flight tracking website.

More than 2 million people pass through airport security checkpoints on a typical day, according to Transportation Security Administration data. On Thursday, the agency screened nearly 2.5 million people. Amid delays and cancellations on Friday evening, many passengers were taken off flights or told to go home.

According to FlightRadar24, an aviation tracking site, there were more than 1,000 airborne aircraft bound for U.S. airports during the nationwide ground stop. According to the flight tracking app Flighty, there were more than 30,000 departures and arrivals scheduled for the remainder of the day.

At least some of the airborne flights appeared to be landing amid the stoppage. About half an hour after the ground stop was declared, planes could be seen landing at O’Hare International Airport.

But passengers waiting to take off were stuck in limbo.

In the Denver airport, passengers were taken off their flights with their suitcases. A handful began rebooking travel for the next day. But most waited patiently for any kind of update. A Southwest flight attendant announced that the airline expected an update in 30 minutes.

Before the advisory was published, the F.A.A. halted flights to Chicago’s O’Hare and Midway airports, citing equipment problems, and reported equipment-related departure delays at Newark, Las Vegas, Teterboro, Orlando, Houston and Phoenix.

Friday’s ground stop is only the third such nationwide moratorium on flights in recent history. The F.A.A. issued nationwide ground stops previously on Sept. 11, 2001, in the wake of the terrorist attack on the World Trade Center in New York, and on Jan. 11, 2023, due to an outage in the F.A.A.’s system to alert pilots to safety issues.

Christine Chung, Niraj Chokshi, Lisa Lerer and Robert Chiarito contributed reporting.

item.title: How Does a 74-Year-Old in Argentina Escape House Arrest on the Fifth Floor?
item.description:
Time was running out for Leonardo Bertulazzi. After decades of safe harbor in Argentina, Mr. Bertulazzi, a former member of a far-left militant group that kidnapped and murdered Italy’s prime minister in 1978, faced imminent extradition back to Italy.

In Europe, a 27-year prison sentence for terrorism-related crimes awaited Mr. Bertulazzi, according to Argentina’s defense ministry.

Mr. Bertulazzi, 74, was placed in house arrest. The police were stationed across the street from the 5th-floor apartment he shared with his wife in Buenos Aires, Argentina’s capital. He’d had three strokes in the last two years, his lawyer said, and he was forced to wear an ankle monitor.

None of that seemed to stop Mr. Bertulazzi from planning his escape.

On Tuesday, while much of the Buenos Aires’ law enforcement apparatus was focused on the visit by Pope Leo, two police officers checked on Mr. Bertulazzi during a routine shift change, according to an official with knowledge of an investigation into Mr. Bertulazzi’s flight who was not authorized to speak publicly.

But this time, when the officers rang the apartment’s doorbell, nobody answered. Investigators believe Mr. Bertulazzi had escaped between 6 a.m. and 8 a.m. that morning.

Mr. Bertulazzi’s ankle monitor still showed he was at the apartment, the official said. A search revealed a metal box holding a mess of wires plugged into an outlet, prompting the officers to call an explosives disposal unit, according to the official.

Argentina’s defense ministry said Mr. Bertulazzi was charged with possessing explosives in connection with his activities with the Red Brigades, the Italian terrorist group that in 1978 kidnapped and assassinated Aldo Moro, the Italian prime minister at the time.

After the all-clear, officers opened the box and found the monitor wrapped around a plastic tube, the official said, which had been coated in animal fat to trick moisture sensors and stuffed with a type of heating pad often used for back pain — creating a contraption that approximated a human leg.

At the fifth-floor window, officers found climbing ropes and a harness, the official with knowledge of the investigation said, adding that Mr. Bertulazzi had rappelled down to a second-floor terrace on another property before running across rooftops, crossing through an empty lot and climbing over a gate.

Closed-circuit footage, shared in local media and confirmed by the official, showed a man dressed in dark clothes tumbling over the side of a green metal fence on a cobblestone street. In the footage, the white-haired figure slammed onto the pavement, stood up and took a moment to rest, leaning against a wall and limping around.

His lawyer, who had argued that his client’s health was too poor for him to withstand prison in Italy, said escape was a natural choice for Mr. Bertulazzi. “Given his age and health condition, honestly, I understand him,” said the lawyer, Rodolfo Yanzon.

Days later, Argentine authorities are still searching for Mr. Bertulazzi. The defense ministry has offered a reward of 20 million pesos, or about $13,000, for information that leads to his recapture. If captured, Mr. Yanzon said, Mr. Bertulazzi would likely be charged with evading justice and placed in jail pending extradition.

Mr. Bertulazzi was part of the Red Brigades, a Marxist-Leninist paramilitary organization that conducted robberies, assaults and assassinations in the 1970s as part of a campaign to foment revolution in Italy. The group is most famous for kidnapping Mr. Moro in March 1978. The Red Brigades held him for nearly two months before fatally shooting him and leaving his body in a car trunk in Rome.

As a high-ranking member of the Red Brigades, Mr. Bertulazzi helped coordinate that kidnapping and others, Argentina’s national security ministry said in a statement in 2024.

The authorities first arrested Mr. Bertulazzi in Argentina in 2002. He was later released, and within two years he was granted refugee status and protections from extradition. But in 2024, Mr. Bertulazzi was arrested after the election of the current president, Javier Milei, a right-wing leader who promised tough-on-crime policies.

“This arrest reflects Argentina’s commitment to the values ​​of democracy and the rule of law, and demonstrates to the world its firm resolve not to tolerate unpunished murderers,” the security ministry’s 2024 statement said.

After a lengthy legal battle, courts this month had cleared the way for Mr. Bertulazzi to be extradited, as Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, had requested.

item.title: Chiclayo, Pope Leo’s Other Home, Comes Out in Force to Welcome Father Robert
item.description:
It was hard to believe that anyone who lived in Chiclayo, Peru, was not lining its streets on Friday.

As the motorcade of Pope Leo XIV, who has been in South America for over a week, made its way through the city that he calls one of his homes, an almost unbroken stream of people stood by the roadside, waving, holding signs and clutching white and yellow balloons, the colors of the Vatican flag.

The last time many of them saw him, he was “Padre Robert” — Father Robert — but now they jubilantly welcomed him back as Papa Leon.

A month after being diagnosed with cancer and undergoing surgery to remove a lobe of his right lung, Leo arrived at the destination that made this 12-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru a true homecoming.

For eight years, Leo — then known as Robert Prevost — served as bishop of Chiclayo, a coastal city where he is remembered for working side by side with the Red Cross during devastating floods or driving for hours to get to parishioners in the highlands.

When he stepped out on the balcony in St. Peter’s Square after being elected pope last year, the one community he mentioned was his “dear Chiclayo.” It was while serving here that he became a Peruvian citizen.

After his plane landed Friday morning at an air base, Leo stepped onto a red carpet and greeted several dignitaries with hugs, rather than his typical handshakes. While a brass band played and dancers performed a traditional “marinera norteña,” a folk dance from northern Peru, the pope stood watching, his face crumpling slightly as if he was trying to control his emotions.

Before Leo arrived, a construction worker died on Wednesday while working on an arc meant to welcome the pope. A spokesman for the diocese of Chiclayo did not return a request for comment about the death.

On Friday, the authorities estimated that about a million people lined the streets of a metropolitan area with a population of less than 900,000. Another 500,000 people, some of whom had staked out a spot the night before, gathered on an open dirt field near a fishing village outside the city, standing for hours under an intense sun to celebrate morning Mass with the pope.

“The Chiclayan pope!” yelled some of the faithful who stood behind barriers. Others hailed Leo like a soccer hero, chanting “Olé, Olé, Olé.” Hawkers sold pope-themed keychains, calendars, T-shirts, photos and posters with Leo’s image, while red fire trucks drove through the crowds spraying people with water to keep them cool. Two men carried a large portrait of Leo they had made using bottle caps.

To secure a spot on the field where they could see the pope, Miriam Chávez, 38, from Chiclayo, and her three children had camped out since midnight. “We didn’t want to miss him,” she said. “He’s worth the wait.”

The pope’s visit, said Cristian Velázquez, 28, came at a crucial time for the city, given “there’s a lot of crime, hunger, and people left to fend for themselves.”

Mr. Velázquez was joined by a dozen fellow motorcycle delivery workers who had images of the pope on the thermal backpacks they used to carry goods. He said that he was worried about the damage that the El Niño weather phenomenon might inflict and hoped the pope “blesses everyone, because right now, more than ever, we need faith and peace.”

When Leo arrived to the Mass site, his pope mobile circulated swiftly through the crowd but missed a large section, prompting a stream of people to rush into a path that led to the stage. Police and a group of volunteers wearing saffron yellow T-shirts clasped arms to create a barrier and push them back before the start of the Mass.

But as the service started, a hush settled over the crowd and the people welcomed their pope home with the sound of “Amen,” rippling across the field.

item.title: In Canada, Watching the N.H.L. Has Become Expensive and Cumbersome
item.description:
The National Hockey League season is less than two months old, and much of the focus in Canada has been on how expensive it is to attend games, and how costly and cumbersome it has become to watch them on television.

Attendance has fallen in several markets, including Edmonton, where Connor McDavid has an astonishing 49 points in 20 games and is on pace to challenge Wayne Gretzky’s single-season scoring record of 215 points.

This week, The Globe and Mail reported that three TV providers had filed a complaint with the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission asking Rogers Sportsnet to reverse its decision to put more than 50 Monday night N.H.L. games behind a paywall on its streaming service for an extra $13 a month.

Further increasing the cost and complexity of watching hockey, Wednesday night games are on Prime Video. TSN broadcasts some regional games with blackouts, and a subscription to NHL Centre Ice is needed to watch out-of-market games.

Until this season, the N.H.L. could be found for free.

In June, the CBC and Rogers Sportsnet announced that the national broadcaster would no longer air N.H.L. games on Saturday nights, a first in 75 years, ending the cultural institution “Hockey Night in Canada.” Last month, the CBC announced it would begin airing Professional Women’s Hockey League games when its season begins in December.

When the news broke, we asked Canada Letter readers to send us their thoughts and memories of “Hockey Night.” The response was overwhelming, and we’d like to share some today. (Responses have been edited for length and clarity.)

“For my childhood in the '60s and ’70s, ‘Hockey Night in Canada’ wasn’t a TV show. It was Saturday night, the once a week chance to see an N.H.L. game on TV. One game. It might as well have been church. For my father and I, it was our greatest bonding experience. We could talk about the game together, watch the game together, anticipate the game — together. And hope for that ultimate fan prize: a bench-clearing brawl.” — Allen Gibson

“I grew up playing hockey in central New York state. When cable TV came to the area, the biggest selling point was that our cable network would carry a station from Kingston, Ontario. The only thing that I do remember clearly is that every Saturday night we watched ‘Hockey Night in Canada.’ It was like winning the lottery every week.” — Brian Goldblatt

“I was born the day of the first ‘Hockey Night in Canada’ broadcast on Nov. 1, 1952. One of my first memories as a young boy is sitting with dad in the basement on Saturday night breathlessly waiting for Foster Hewitt’s voice and wondering what the score might be (the early broadcasts started mid-game). Hockey has been in my blood since then, and I am both blessed (1967!) and cursed (59 years!) by my support of the Maple Leafs. The demise of this CBC broadcast is the direct result of the fragmentation of sports broadcasting. I fear that this continuing trend may have the longer term effect of alienating fans. It has for me with hockey, after a lifetime of living with this beautiful game.” — John Butler

“This is shattering. I have just started to follow hockey, and watching these broadcasts has made me feel part of the hockey community more than anything else. So sick of the ESPN effect on sports — slick programming that makes every sporting event seem like every other sporting event. Canadians, and true hockey fans everywhere, should be outraged by this loss, and clamor to bring it back. Hockey’s roots in the Great North should be preserved.” — Doyla Rosati

“My best memory of ‘Hockey Night in Canada’ relates to the old theme song, by the late Dolores Claman. There was a time, not that long ago, when you could easily find other Canadians in an overseas airport just by whistling the first few notes of the theme. As if on cue, another Canadian would respond with the next notes. It was always a magical moment when traveling.” — Michael Olsen

“It is so depressing that corporate greed can wipe out one of the most iconic cultural traditions in Canada. Even though I’m not the biggest hockey fan, my family was. And every Saturday night growing up at home I’d hear the familiar opening tune of ‘Hockey Night in Canada.’ It is one of my most heartwarming memories of watching my family around the TV cheering on the Leafs. To this day, that music comes on and it reminds me I’m part of that glorious Canadian tradition too. Especially at this time when celebrating Canadian pride is at its strongest in my lifetime.” — Alida Stevenson

“In the late 1980s we had a satellite dish (one of those big ones) while living in Colorado. We ended up watching a lot of CBC programming because it was free, including ‘Hockey Night in Canada.’ I knew almost nothing about hockey. But I started watching from time to time, especially after the Quebec Nordiques came to Denver and became the Colorado Avalanche. ‘Hockey Night’ taught me about hockey enough that I could enjoy it.” — Karen Wydeven

“There are a lot of varied opinions on CBC’s role in Canada, however in this matter, I think many agree that it will be a very large loss, but also a possible turning point for our public broadcaster. I spent a lot of nights watching CBC’s ‘H.N.I.C.' or listening to CBC on the radio for the games. Hopefully CBC will take the opportunity to become the national broadcaster for the P.W.H.L., something I wish had been when I was a young girl. How incredible it would have been for 5-year-old me to have watched women play the sport I love so much. Something I now wish for younger female athletes.” — Tammy Jakeman

“As an avid fan during the Canadiens’ amazing run in the ’70s I wanted to watch ‘Hockey Night in Canada’ on Saturdays. My dad didn’t think it was appropriate for a teenage girl to be watching hockey. He didn’t know I listened to almost every game on the radio during the week. So I made a deal with him, I would crochet in front of the television if I could watch with him.” — Cremilda Dias

“I grew up in Montreal in a family that came from a small Greek island: Naxos. My grandfather came over in 1907 but we had quite a few relatives in the city who were recent immigrants and still struggled to speak either English or French. On Saturday nights we often went to family functions in the homes of relatives who hadn’t been in Canada that long and were still emotionally tied to the village. By 8 o’clock, the men would gather around the black and white TV to watch whatever game was on. None of them ever missed it, especially when they were together and the Montreal Canadiens were playing. They argued passionately about every play, every lost opportunity, the strength and weaknesses of each player, entirely in Greek. It seemed that as soon as they stepped off the boat and started their lives in Montreal they discovered ‘Hockey Night in Canada.’ It became their doorway to their new country.” — Emmanuel Hadzipetros

“Born in 1960, I watched ‘Hockey Night in Canada’ growing up. I grew tired of the violence and watch it only occasionally during the season and playoffs. I am thrilled that the dropping of it will help promote more coverage of the women’s game.” — Susan Funnell

“As a farm kid growing up in small town southern Alberta in the early 1960s we had one station, CBC, and ‘Hockey Night in Canada’ was a Saturday night ritual. If the atmospheric gods were smiling on us, we were graced with a static filled black and white image, but at least the audio was good. To this day hearing the theme magically transports me back to small town Alberta surrounded by my brothers and sister and cold dark winter nights. It’s the end of an era.” — Laurence Torsher

“It represents a slice of Canadian culture that is only a slice, as the success of the P.W.H.L. shows. The negative effects of the male professional hockey machine are well-documented. I’m proud of how the CBC is a platform for less-popular sports, like women’s hockey and soccer, volleyball and softball, and the non-hockey Olympics. These athletes compete for a pittance and often have to support themselves on the side. I think it helps keep the ‘sport’ of it in perspective.” — Tim Dyck

“In 1969, overpacked car driven by my new French Canadian husband, we went from my family home in Connecticut to Montreal. I’d had Latin and Spanish in school and my husband had very little English. We met one year before in the German pub on the Expo Islands. Twelve months later, after long distance calls, torturous letters written and read with bilingual dictionaries, and two weeks of intensive French classes, we married. We lived in a three-story apartment in the middle unit with the French sounds of the neighbors’ radios seeping into the rooms. However, most of my French that year came from ‘Hockey Night in Canada.’ We watched it at the grandparents’ where the large extended family gathered on Saturday evenings to cheer encouragement. I also learned a couple of cuss words when things did not go well.” — Carol Ann St-Jean

“I lived in Montreal during the war Vietnam War, and later Vancouver. What surprised me at the time, being a Yank with no interest in sports in general of any kind, how totally captivating ‘H.N.I.C.’ was for Canadians. Everyone, certainly among the Canadians I worked with and socialized with, was home watching hockey on telly that night, and talking about the games the following day. I also recall that crime stats dropped to almost zero on ‘H.N.I.C.’ days. The entire cultural spectacle was lost on me at the time, yet another indication of how little us Yanks knew and understood Canada at the time.” — Dick Matthews

“When I was growing up in Northern Ontario, ‘Hockey Night in Canada’ was two nights a week, both Wednesday and Saturday. On school nights I was allowed to watch one period, on Saturdays two. But each bedtime was the same. I would kneel by my bed and pray that the Leafs won, so my dad wouldn’t be sad.” — Rhonda Wright

“As a now-elderly American I first heard ‘H.N.I.C.’ on static filled radio under the covers when I should have been sleeping. As an adult in the Detroit suburbs, it came to me from CBC Windsor. For me it was and remained the gold standard in sports broadcasting. Whatever will replace it on Saturday night will fail to match the memories. We live in an age of change, and must adapt. But some changes we can regret, and this will sting, at least for awhile.” — Joe Sher

Shawna Richer is the Canada editor at The Times. She lives in Toronto and has been editing and writing about sports for more than 25 years.

By Mark Colley

Caleb Linton, 7, had a liver transplant at Toronto’s Hospital for Sick Children when he was 6 months old. The doctors, he says, saved his life. That’s why he’s here.

“Here” is a room in the old wing of SickKids, where Linton is performing this month in an adventurous theatrical production that unfolds across eight floors and more than a dozen rooms of the working hospital. The SickKids Foundation is staging the show, which features 16 professional actors and a rotating cast of former patients, to kick off a fund-raising initiative with a goal of 2.5 billion Canadian dollars.

Michael Rubinoff, who produced the hit musical “Come From Away” on Broadway and the West End, is behind the performance. He says this show is “the most profound experience I’ve had as a producer.” It is also among the most challenging.

Six separate audience groups move through different parts of the hospital while the story unfolds. Monica Dottor, playing a doctor, meets one group in a hallway, while PJ Prudat, dressed as a therapeutic clown, wheelies down the same hallway with another.

The choreography is orchestrated from a dark office tucked away on the sixth floor, where the stage manager Kate Sandeson watches video feeds from each room. She is one of six stage mangers on the production, more than the largest professional productions in Toronto, Rubinoff said.

A project this complex would normally take two years to put together. The creative team did it in six months. The Toronto director Mitchell Cushman, a co-creator, likened it to “building the airplane while you’re flying.”

The SickKids Foundation has raised about 1 billion Canadian dollars so far in its 10-year campaign, which began in 2023. “It’s a huge number,” said Jennifer Bernard, president and C.E.O. of the foundation, and it required an equally ambitious launch. She has seen the show 10 times.

Few members of the public, however, will get the chance. Most of the 21 performances, spread over three weeks for audiences of 100, are for donors and hospital staff members. Only one, on Nov. 20, is open to the public, and a lottery for one of 42 available pairs of tickets has drawn more than a thousand entries.

Mark Colley is a reporter for The Times based in Vancouver. He covers breaking news and Canada.

Trekking through the wilds of the Yukon territory, the American novelist Maggie Shipstead reconsiders her relationship to aging and risk.

Four grizzly bears were responsible for the attack that killed two women in British Columbia this month, wildlife authorities said this week. The sow and her three cubs were captured over the weekend, and forensic testing, including the examination of animal DNA, conclusively linked them to the attack.

Giant roadside attractions — like Tyra the Tyrannosaurus of Drumheller, Alberta — have helped put hundreds of communities on the map. What happens when their novelty fades and costs pile up?

Stormy weather that battered the Pacific Northwest and southwestern Canada spread during the week, bringing the region’s first major dose of winter rains.

How are we doing?We’re eager to have your thoughts about this newsletter and events in Canada in general. Please send them to nytcanada@nytimes.com.

item.title: Here’s the latest.
item.description:
The Eurovision Song Contest will crown its first Asia champion in Bangkok on Saturday, in an event that will test whether a high-camp singing competition with an ardent fan base can appeal to audiences in a new market.

The inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia comprises artists and original songs from 11 countries: Bangladesh, Bhutan, Cambodia, Laos, Malaysia, Mongolia, Nepal, the Philippines, South Korea, Thailand and Vietnam. It will be live-streamed on YouTube at 8:30 p.m. local time (8:30 a.m. Eastern) and broadcast by television stations across the region.

Eurovision has been a fixture of the European cultural calendar since it began in 1956. Past winners include Sweden’s ABBA and the Canadian chanteuse Celine Dion, who represented Switzerland in 1988.

Asian artists have readily embraced the kitschy outfits and spectacular sets that are part of Eurovision tradition, with costumes that include traditional dress, as well as feathered capes and sequined corsets. Malaysia’s performer plans to enter the stage in a giant teardrop.

But the Eurovision format has not been tested in Asia. Fans and regional partners have expressed concern in recent weeks that budget constraints, production issues and weak audience demand could imperil the spinoff. Organizers say the contest could take time to build an audience.

“It would be profoundly arrogant to think that just because we have a heritage brand and a huge global audience for the European show, that we would walk in and demand it to be the same here,” said Martin Green, the European Broadcasting Union’s director of the Eurovision Song Contest. “Like any new thing, it needs to find its roots.”

Two previous attempts to take the competition to Asia were abandoned by the European Broadcasting Union, which owns Eurovision, and its partners in the region. A Eurovision spinoff in the United States, NBC’s American Song Contest, ran for one season in 2022.

The Asian edition kicking off on Saturday is far smaller than its European counterpart. Eurovision organizers said they were in talks with more countries to join future seasons. They include China, Japan and India, whose music industries have global reach.

“Bringing the world together through music is a fundamentally good idea,” Mr. Green said. “Europe shouldn’t keep it to itself.”

Here’s what we’re covering:

Politics: Geopolitics have long intruded on the European edition of the Eurovision Song Contest, but they were not really a factor as the event prepared to expand into Asia. Read more ›

Voting process: Each artist will receive half their scores from professional juries in each country, and the other half from public voting on the Eurovision Asia website. Viewers are allowed to vote for artists from at least three other countries — not their own.

item.title: Geopolitics Looms Over Eurovision, but Not Its Asian Edition
item.description:
Geopolitics have long intruded on the Eurovision Song Contest. But they were not really a factor as the event prepared to expand into Asia for the first time.

That was still true as of Saturday evening, as the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia was about to start in Bangkok.

Over the decades, Eurovision organizers have insisted that the contest is nonpolitical. Its organizers impose rules governing lyrics, political symbols and what can be broadcast. Even so, wars and diplomatic disputes have shaped who gets to sing, who stays home and what broadcasters are willing to air.

“Politics is why we watch Eurovision,” said Dean Vuletic, a historian of the show at the University of Luxembourg.

Here are some examples of geopolitics bleeding into the European edition of the contest:

In 2009, less than a year after fighting a war with Russia, the former Soviet republic of Georgia planned to send a disco song called “We Don’t Wanna Put In” to Eurovision. Eurovision’s organizers said that the apparent dig at Vladimir Putin, then Russia’s prime minister, had to go. Georgia pulled out instead of changing it.

In 2017, Russia pulled out of the contest in Kyiv after Ukraine barred its singer from entering the country. And five years later, after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Eurovision barred Russia altogether.

In 2024, the war in Gaza triggered mass protests over Israel’s participation. A bitter dispute over government influence on voting followed in 2025, and there were boycotts of the contest by five countries in 2026, the biggest crisis in Eurovision’s 70-year history.

The 11 Asian countries that sent artists to Saturday’s show have plenty of offstage geopolitical friction.

Cambodia, for example, is set to sing in Thailand’s capital less than a year after a border war between the two neighbors killed dozens and displaced hundreds of thousands. As fighting picked up last year, Cambodia withdrew its athletes from the Southeast Asian Games in Thailand, citing safety concerns.

But none of that has translated into a Eurovision controversy.

Mr. Vuletic said he expects Eurovision Asia to become a more visible platform for politics if the event continues over the next few years, drawing a wider audience and raising the stakes for countries taking part.

For now, some of Asia’s biggest powers are conspicuously absent from the lineup. Broadcasters from China, Japan and India discussed participating but did not sign up before the entry deadline, said Assaf Blecher, the contest’s executive producer. Pakistan and Indonesia are also absent.

China’s relations with Japan have been strained by a diplomatic dispute over Taiwan, which spilled into pop culture last year when Beijing canceled Japanese concerts and restricted films. China also has overlapping maritime claims in the South China Sea with the Philippines, Vietnam and Malaysia — countries that are all competing on Saturday.

Taiwan’s absence spares the organizers potentially sensitive decisions about names and flags. Beijing claims the self-governing island as its territory and opposes its treatment as an independent country. Such symbols have proved contentious at Eurovision, which in 2024 barred its audience from carrying Palestinian flags while permitting those of participating countries, including Israel.

Eurovision’s organizers have said the competition is “not a contest between governments.” But maintaining that distinction involves decisions about both what performers can sing and what broadcasters air.

The European contest’s rules prohibit political lyrics, speeches and gestures, and entrants may be asked to submit new songs or rewrite offending words. In 2024, organizers required Israel to change the title and lyrics of “October Rain,” which appeared to reference the Hamas-led Oct. 7 attacks. The song became “Hurricane.”

For all the trouble it can bring, the breadth of representation has also been part of Eurovision’s appeal since its founding in 1956, as an experiment in international television and an effort to bring Cold War Europe together. Bosnia and Herzegovina debuted in 1993 while Sarajevo, its capital, was under siege. Its singer, Fazla, told The New York Times in 2022 that he had escaped barefoot under sniper fire after his shoes became stuck in the mud.

“Eurovision is about representing your nation,” he said, “about giving yourself a platform to bring your story into the living rooms of normal people.”

Eurovision is not the only song contest to offer that platform. Russia revived the Cold War-era Intervision contest in 2025, after its exclusion from Eurovision over the invasion of Ukraine. It promoted the new competition as a showcase for what the Kremlin calls “traditional values.”

Vietnam’s Duc Phuc won that contest in Moscow.

On Saturday in Bangkok, another Vietnamese pop star, Toc Tien, will be first onstage at Eurovision Asia.

item.title: In French Election, Centrists Eye a Judo Star and a Central Banker
item.description:
When Teddy Riner, a judo champion and one of France’s most popular athletes, announced this week that he would run for president, it was less a game changer than a welcome diversion. For all of his appeal, Mr. Riner, 37, is unlikely to win the race to replace President Emmanuel Macron next spring.

Yet his quixotic candidacy reveals a hard truth about France’s presidential campaign. Five months before voters go to the polls, many are eager, even desperate, for a fresh face to upend a race that looks increasingly as if it’s on a glide path to the election of France’s first far-right government since World War II.

The main far-right candidate, Marine Le Pen, has held a commanding lead over all her rivals for months — a lead that has only been reinforced by weeks of protests, marred by violence, that have shaken France. The most prominent center-right candidate, Édouard Philippe, has faded in the polls as the unrest has sharpened the appeal of far-right calls for law and order and left-wing calls for social justice.

Another beneficiary of the upheaval is a far-left firebrand, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who now appears to be the likeliest candidate to advance into a second round against Ms. Le Pen in France’s two-round system. As things currently stand, French voters would be confronted with a choice between two poles of the political spectrum.

Centrist voters are “afraid of being confronted with a duel between Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon,” said Jean-Daniel Lévy, deputy director of Toluna France, a polling firm. These voters, he said, are an “orphan electorate,” lacking an inspiring candidate, and are “still looking for someone.”

Raphaël LLorca, an analyst at the Jean-Jaurès Foundation, a left-leaning research group in Paris, said the search for a white knight showed “the panic of the centrist bloc.” He added, “It is clear that the election is slipping away from them.”

Mr. Riner’s name is not the only one tantalizing frustrated centrists. Christine Lagarde, a French lawyer and former finance minister, announced her resignation as president of the European Central Bank last month, saying she wanted the freedom to weigh in on political debates. She has ruled out a run for the presidency, but that hasn’t stopped French newspapers from speculating that she might still join the race.

Dominique de Villepin, a former foreign minister and prime minister who declared France’s refusal to join the American-led invasion of Iraq in 2003, is weighing a bid. So is François Hollande, a center-left former president who left office in 2017 with the lowest approval rating of any president since France’s current system of government, known as the Fifth Republic, was founded in 1958.

Among declared candidates, two other fresh faces have recently spiked in the polls: David Lisnard, the mayor of Cannes, a socially conservative free marketeer with a slick social media profile; and Raphaël Glucksmann, a left-leaning member of the European Parliament, who recently won a primary among candidates on the center left.What they have in common is that neither worked for Mr. Macron, who, in his waning months in office, is rivaling Mr. Hollande for unpopularity. The three most established center-right candidates — Mr. Philippe, Gabriel Attal and Bruno Retailleau — all served in top jobs in Macron governments. In an election driven by change, analysts say, they are tarnished by that association.

“David Lisnard and Raphaël Glucksmann are not accountable for the past,” said Mr. Lévy, deputy director of the polling firm.

Mr. Lisnard, a onetime journalist who is the son of a professional soccer player, was a vice president of the main right-wing party, the Republicans, and started his own party, New Energy, in 2021. Mr. Glucksmann, a former documentary filmmaker whose father, André Glucksmann, was a famous philosopher, ran for office on a list of Socialist candidates. But he has never been a member of the Socialists, having started his own party, Place Publique, in 2018.

In the most recent poll by Ipsos, Raphaël Glucksmann drew 13 percent, equal to that of Mr. Philippe but behind Mr. Mélenchon, at 17 percent, and Ms. Le Pen, at 33.5 percent. Mr. Lisnard drew 6.5 percent; in other recent polls, he has been as high as 9 percent.

Both men face an uphill struggle, according to analysts: Mr. Lisnard, because he is jostling in a crowded center-right field; Mr. Glucksmann, because the center left has all but withered as a political force in France.

Analysts are also skeptical about a Lagarde candidacy — and not just because she told the French paper La Croix in September that running “would not be a good idea at all.” She cited her age, 70, and the demands of the job.

Philippe Marlière, an expert on French politics at University College London, said Ms. Lagarde’s technocratic style and pro-European tilt would be a liability in an election fueled by populism and nationalism. “This speculation tells us more about the crisis of the French center right,” he said.

Thierry Breton, a former commissioner at the European Union whose name has also come up as a potential candidate, said centrists were struggling because voters were turned off by conventional politicians, with detailed policy agendas, and seemed “willing to vote more and more for a figure or character.”

Enter Mr. Riner, a five-time Olympic gold medalist in judo who has never held elected office. He was born in Guadeloupe, a French territory in the Caribbean, to parents who moved to mainland France in the early 1990s. Mr. Riner has cast his life story as a testament to France’s greatness and vowed to be a unifying force. While his policy positions are a work in progress, he bills himself as a candidate of “neither the right nor the left.”

On paper, he would appear an even longer shot than Ms. Lagarde. But Mr. Lévy noted that Mr. Riner would appeal to younger voters flocking to Mr. Mélenchon, the far-left leader, who has been a fixture at student-led protests. Certainly, none of the candidates can match Mr. Riner’s outsider status.

“I hear anger, which some people echo with a lot of negativity, and from the mouths of people who no longer have ambition or the desire to think big,” Mr. Riner said in an interview with the French paper Le Parisien. “But France is a great country. It allowed me to become the person I am.”

Among those who welcomed Mr. Riner’s campaign was Mr. Macron, who famously emerged as a fresh face midway through the 2017 election. Speaking to a French broadcaster, he said he was “very happy” that Mr. Riner was joining the fray.

“It can only benefit the country,” Mr. Macron said.

Ségolène Le Stradic contributed reporting.

item.title: Europe Haggles Over Who Will Represent It in Talks With Russia
item.description:
European leaders have waited on the margins of negotiations to end Russia’s war in Ukraine for months, eyeing a seat at the table. Now they finally expect to get one, and they don’t know who should sit in it.

“If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation,” Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law and one of his two envoys, said on Thursday.

Mr. Kushner’s dig reflected a harsh — and, for Europe, potentially embarrassing — reality that internal divisions could cost European officials time and influence. Mr. Kushner and his fellow lead U.S. negotiator, Steve Witkoff, pushed this week to add the Europeans to the talks after Russia insisted during discussions in the United Arab Emirates that postwar security in Europe be a topic of negotiation.

Russian negotiators made it clear during the talks with Ukraine and the United States that as a condition of ending the war, they want Europe to change how it protects itself. Russia has a record of pushing to pare back NATO operations near its border.

European officials have rejected those suggestions, insisting that the continent, not the Kremlin, decides its own security. But Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff expressed openness to expanding the scope of the talks to try to break the impasse on discussions about the war.

“I don’t want someone to talk about our European house, if they are not living in that house,” Luc Frieden, prime minister of Luxembourg, said in an interview on Friday.

Naming a lead negotiator would give Europe a voice in discussions about its own future, while failing to identify someone quickly might make the continent appear weak and fragmented. How the Ukraine war is settled could reverberate across Europe for decades — either containing the threat of Russian expansionism or emboldening it.

“Europe really needs to pay attention,” President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine warned dozens of leaders from across the continent assembled in Dublin for a summit on Thursday. European Union leaders will debate who should represent them on Friday at a lunch in the Irish capital. Mr. Zelensky is pushing Europe to choose someone by the end of the month, possibly as soon as a meeting of Ukraine’s allies next Thursday in Germany.

The issue grew more pressing late on Thursday. Mr. Kushner told reporters at an air base in Dublin, after a meeting with the Kremlin, that Russian officials had been asked about having European negotiators at the table and were “willing to give it a try.” Mr. Zelensky, standing alongside him, added that “next time, next meeting,” Europe will be on the “negotiation team.”

Even with such high stakes, picking a representative, or even a small group to speak for Europe, has become a herculean lift.

Small nations in the European Union do not always trust big ones to reflect their interests. Britain and Norway, which have a financial and security stake, are not part of the union. Eastern nations bordering Russia doubt that western ones understand the depth of the menace they face.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk of Poland said on Thursday, “Under no circumstances will we allow new security rules for this part of the world to be established over our heads, without Poland or Europe having a say.”

European officials have already warned not to expect an immediate choice, though nominations are pouring in.

António Costa, president of the European Union’s political leadership arm, comes up frequently as a possibility. Mr. Frieden, the Luxembourg prime minister, has suggested that Mr. Costa should be the bloc’s representative. Prime Minister Andrej Babis of the Czech Republic threw out a handful of names, including Mr. Tusk and Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni of Italy.

Several leaders suggested that they were more likely to settle on a group than a single person.

“It’s not necessarily one person, but there should be a clear, coherent leadership, from the European Union, at that table,” Micheal Martin, the Irish leader, told reporters this week.

One possibility could be a team of negotiators from Europe’s large nations, Britain and NATO, led by Mr. Costa as a central figure. Mr. Costa himself alluded to a potential grouping.

“Europe’s security cannot be discussed without a European voice at the table — that European voice needs to be a team effort between European nations, the European Union and NATO,” he said.

Two European diplomats said that one concern is that Mr. Costa may lack the international stature to impress the Russians and Americans. The diplomats spoke on condition of anonymity to describe private conversations.

Mr. Costa has long argued that the European Union must be represented in discussions because the bloc controls a large set of sanctions against Russia, which Moscow wants rolled back. Another factor is Ukraine’s potential E.U. membership, which Kyiv wants as a security guarantee.

Complicating matters, many European officials have opposed even opening discussions with Russia before Moscow agrees to a cease-fire.

When Mr. Costa’s office tried in June to reopen lines of communication with Russia, France and Germany criticized him for overreaching.

These discussions might unfold differently, the two European diplomats suggested, because the chance of sitting at the table now seems realistic and Europe’s security is clearly on the line.

“We will figure out who to represent Europe,” Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of Denmark said on Thursday. “In democracies, there will be discussions, but I’m pretty sure we will find a way forward.”

That doesn’t mean it won’t be tumultuous.

item.title: Caught Between Killers: Ebola on One Side, Islamic State on the Other
item.description:
So many people are dying of Ebola that their bodies have been stacked, one atop the other, on makeshift racks in a shed by the hospital gate.

The town’s main cemetery is full, so fresh graves are being squeezed in between palm trees by the side of the road.

Medicine, IVs and basic protections have been so scarce that three-quarters of Ebola patients in this besieged Congolese town have died.

The new epicenter of Congo’s fast-spreading outbreak is a region scarred by rebel violence. Responders are struggling to help it.

By Declan Walsh

Photographs by Daniel Berehulak

Declan Walsh and Daniel Berehulak have traveled for weeks through remote towns in eastern Congo to track the spread of Ebola.

Six months on, Ebola continues to hack a deadly trail across eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

When the outbreak was first detected in May, it resembled a single, giant blaze, with infections concentrated in a handful of towns in one province.

It has since morphed into a far bigger, more elusive foe, creeping into eight provinces and splintering into numerous hot spots as its moves through one of the world’s great rainforests.

Instead of one big fire, there are many now, scattered across a vast area about the size of Britain.

Health workers have corralled the virus where it was first detected, but infections are soaring elsewhere. Biakato, a small town deep in the rainforest, suddenly accounted for as many as one-quarter of new cases nationally. Yet its beleaguered residents were left almost entirely on their own, with dangerously little to defend themselves against the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.

“We see the same mistakes as before,” said Dr. Jean-Jacques Muyembe, who helped discover Ebola in 1976 and now heads Congo’s National Institute for Biomedical Research. “It’s as if we were starting from zero. It’s very disappointing.”

And if that were not enough, the campaign to contain the epidemic has run into a terrifying new threat: the Islamic State.

Ebola was already swamping Biakato when I got to the town in mid-October with the photographer Daniel Berehulak. Exhausted health workers reported 300 cases in the span of a month, up from 20 the month before.

But there were only two doctors, they hadn’t been paid in months, and they felt utterly abandoned. The aid workers who would normally pour in and set up an Ebola treatment center were being scared off by rebel fighters who have been terrorizing the region for years.

Their fears were tragically realized in recent days when the rebels, who are affiliated with the Islamic State, killed 106 people in a series of attacks across the region, U.N. officials said. One of the deadliest episodes occurred 25 miles south of Biakato, where militants torched homes, shops and health facilities, forcing Ebola patients to flee their beds. Thousands of residents also fled in an exodus likely to further spread the disease.

Even by the standards of eastern Congo, where conflict has raged for three decades, the fighters — from a group called the Allied Democratic Forces, or A.D.F. — are considered especially brutal. They roam the sprawling forests, periodically springing from their hiding places to mount attacks. Civilians are beheaded, mutilated and abducted. Children are forced to fight with the group. Mass killings have taken place at funerals and churches.

In 2019, the group pledged allegiance to the Islamic State, and by one recent estimate, it is the world’s second-deadliest group for civilians. Now, its terror tactics are hobbling the fight against Ebola.

A tentative effort to rescue Biakato is underway. Aid groups are using helicopters to fly over the perilous forests and have begun to build a treatment center. Even so, the local volunteers battling to hold back the tide of infections say they are in an impossible bind.

“We’ve got the A.D.F. on one side, and Ebola on the other,” said Jean-Lefranc Sakara, head of a Red Cross team that collects the Ebola dead from their houses. “We are well and truly caught in the middle.”

Daniel and I reached Biakato after a jolting two-hour ride through the rainforest. A wall of trees rose on either side, interrupted in places by ghost villages, their deserted buildings barely visible behind grass and weeds.

The fighters started preying on this forested corridor five years ago, ambushing passing traffic and raiding settlements. Most residents have since fled.

“It wasn’t safe for children any more,” said a man who suddenly emerged from the bushes, “so everyone moved to Biakato.” He hurried away, vanishing into the tall grass.

This muddy track, running 85 miles through the rainforest, has become the central artery of the outbreak. Cases are soaring in the towns of Beni and Mambasa, at either end of the road. Halfway along it lies Biakato.
