Since May, more than 5,000 people have died in this outbreak, and experts fear it is growing so fast that it may surpass the devastating West Africa epidemic of 2014 to 2016, the largest on record, which killed more than 11,000. As recently as September, experts thought they were getting a handle on this one, but in recent weeks the transmission rate has risen again, according to official figures obtained by The New York Times, meaning it is still out of control.

Here in the district traversed by the Beni-Mambasa corridor, the transmission rate is double the average, suggesting that Ebola is spreading largely unchecked, experts say.

As we pressed on, Biakato came into view, its tin roofs sparkling amid the sea of green. On the edge of town, municipal workers guided us through a hand-washing station. In the center, motorbikes roared as people flowed into small shops and gold counters. Farmers dried cacao beans on giant mats, their lucrative crop used to make chocolate.

At the town hospital, chaos reigned. Families clustered by the gate, some wailing, as the bagged bodies of Ebola victims were carried out. An isolation area had been set up inside a pediatric ward. Patients sat listlessly on the steps outside, some visibly weak, separated from a bustling public section by a flimsy strip of orange fencing that did almost nothing to contain the disease.

Ebola patients and their relatives gathered by the fence, chatting at close quarters. One patient shared a bottle of juice with a visitor, passing it back and forth, risking transmission through infected saliva. Conditions were so bad that 75 percent of Ebola patients had died, the town’s records showed.

Espérance Kombi, a mother of seven, had been in the ward for two weeks. She looked stronger than most patients, but was traumatized by the deaths and suffering she had witnessed.

“I need a second heart to endure what I’ve seen in there,” she said, pointing to the ward door. “This one is not enough,” she added, tapping her chest.

Until recently, violence was the most pressing concern in Biakato. In May, fighters with the Islamic State affiliate stormed into the town, killing 21 people. Soldiers from nearby Uganda began patrolling the streets, under an agreement with the Congolese government, to ward off attacks.

But the upheaval continues just outside town. It got so dangerous recently that a group of hunter-gatherers from the forest, whose ancestors had lived there for centuries, took shelter beside the town’s Catholic church.

Alice Gloria, 18, sat on a stoop, still dazed by her ordeal. In September, fighters snatched her and her family from their farm. For four nights, she was marched through the forest, her 1-year-old baby in her arms.

At night, the fighters raped her repeatedly, she said in a whisper. “The older men did it.”

Ms. Gloria escaped on the fifth day, as the fighters attacked another farm. She walked for three days, carrying her daughter, until they reached Biakato. But her husband, Augustin, couldn’t escape with them. He was back in the forest, his fate unknown. “Still no news,” she said.

At first, it seemed that Ebola might bypass Biakato, said Job Bakwata, the town’s chief medical officer. The first recorded case was a gold miner who returned from the town of Mongbwalu in June, then died. But in the months that followed, as the virus ravaged other areas, Biakato had only a dribble of cases: one more in June, 14 in July, 20 in August.

Then in mid-September, infections surged, overwhelming the battered town.

Mr. Sakara, the Red Cross volunteer, threw himself into the response. A onetime seminarian, he had moved to Biakato four years earlier in search of safety. The rebels had attacked his home in the mountains of North Kivu, killing a sister and three brothers. “My grandfather told me to get out,” he said. “We came here to start over.”

After Ebola hit, he dropped everything to lead a small team that collects and disinfects the bodies of Ebola victims. Working that close to the virus was daunting, he said. The volunteers had protective suits but little training, and he felt terrified in the homes of Ebola victims who had just died, mopping up their infected blood or dragging their contaminated mattresses outside.

His team also faced hostility from the very people they are trying to save. Mourners hurled stones as they tried to bury the dead, showering them with insults and accusing them of somehow profiting from the outbreak. “They call it ‘Ebola business,’” he said.

That hostility was a disaster for the effort to stop the virus from spreading further. Ebola victims are at their most contagious after they die, which can turn unmanaged funerals into superspreader events.

Over the previous week, four members of his 12-person team had quit, fearing for their lives, he said. Nobody had stepped forward to replace them. “You cannot imagine what we are going through,” he said.

Rebels and many residents have one thing in common: Both groups were drawn to Biakato by cacao and gold. In a forest clearing outside town, Ismail Mbafumoja plucked a colorful pod from a branch, split it open and scooped out a brown seed coated in white pulp. “Cacao,” he said.

Until recently, his biggest worry was guarding his crop against Islamic State fighters and Congolese soldiers, both of whom he considered a threat. But now he had little time to farm at all because of all the funerals for Ebola’s victims. “I can’t count how many I’ve been to,” he said.

The farmer paused outside a neighbor’s house. Nobody was home, he said, because a child who lived here had just died. “Ebola,” he said.

The care Biakato’s patients so urgently needed could be found just 40 miles away, in Beni.

A treatment center run by Doctors Without Borders offered the gold standard in Ebola care. Doctors in white suits worked in tented wards. Strict safety protocols were observed. There were over 200 staff members, about six per patient. The center even had psychologists to manage patient trauma.

“We’ve learned a lot from previous outbreaks,” said Sam Arnold, the facility’s deputy head.

There was nothing of the sort in Biakato, despite the surging cases. In 2013, four Doctors Without Borders workers were abducted in an A.D.F. raid on a village in North Kivu Province. One escaped after 13 months; the other three have never been found.

The World Health Organization, which is leading the effort to get help to Biakato, has its own painful history in the town. During the last outbreak in this area, in 2019, armed men attacked its guesthouse in Biakato, killing three Ebola responders. Officials blamed the violence on the Mai-Mai, a term for local militias.

That leaves health officials walking a tightrope. Proceed too slowly, and Biakato could become a deep reservoir of Ebola, spreading infection across the region. Move too quickly, and they risk an attack, like a killing or a kidnapping of aid workers, that could collapse the entire effort.

Mistrust among local residents is also a problem. After decades of war, and numerous failed military operations, faith in the government has collapsed, officials said. The same Congolese soldiers who are supposed to protect the community also prey on it, seeking bribes or profiting from gold. When Ebola came along, locals saw the disease as yet another plot to suppress them.

“They don’t trust outsiders,” said Julien Harneis, the United Nations Ebola coordinator in Congo. “Experience has taught them not to.”

As infections began to rise in September, a W.H.O. team returned to Biakato to see how they might help. The omens were ominous, at first. The health workers woke one morning to find a headless sheep dumped outside their hotel — a sign they were not welcome, said Dr. Steve Ahuka, the head of Congo’s Ebola response.

But within weeks, Ebola had become so overwhelming that Biakato’s distrustful leaders were pleading for help.

On Oct. 12, Dr. Ahuka and Catherine Smallwood, a senior W.H.O. official, returned to Biakato to a very different reception. Local leaders formed a circle around Ms. Smallwood and, after apologizing for the 2019 killings, implored her to send help.

“They asked me to put the past in the past,” she recalled. “It was an extremely touching moment.”

Since then, the W.H.O. has deployed officials and revamped the chaotic health center. The Congolese government set up a lab to test patients. Medair, a Swiss aid organization, has sent medics.

And yet, even that may not be enough.

To stamp out the virus, health workers need to trace every known contact of an infected person. That kind of investigative work is impossible in the countryside while the A.D.F. still threatens it.

Dr. Muyembe, the Ebola expert, urged his government to consider what was once unthinkable: reaching out to the Islamic State.

“You absolutely have to find a way to get in touch with these people,” he said. “You have to tell them, ‘This is a risk you face, too.’”

Such an approach, even if exploratory, would be difficult, he admitted. Congo’s government officially refuses to negotiate with the A.D.F., a group the United States has designated as a terrorist organization.

“But we have to do it,” Dr. Muyembe urged.

Otherwise, he said, Ebola “will be impossible to contain.”

On the verge of collapse, Moïse Kalindera, 27, struggled up the steps of the Ebola ward, assisted by a medical worker in a white suit.

For weeks, relatives had been ferrying him from one clinic to another, in an increasingly frantic search for a cure. When he tested positive for Ebola, they refused to believe it.

“We think he has been poisoned,” his sister, Consolée, said as she watched him shuffle through the ward doors.

Mr. Kalindera was placed in a small room with another young man who offered hope of a way out.

Germain Kanyungu, a 31-year-old farmhand, had no illusions about Ebola. After fighting the virus for weeks, he was finally recovering and had just tested negative. One more result like that and he would be free.

He couldn’t wait. “Once I get out of here,” he said, “I’m never coming back to Biakato.”

That night, the two young men got to talking in the lonely Ebola ward, Mr. Kanyungu later recounted. They shared jokes and laughed. Mr. Kanyungu helped his roommate eat and comforted him when he confided his fears of dying.

The next day, Consolée and a brother came to visit. But neither wore any protection, and the brother emptied Mr. Kalindera’s urine bucket with his bare hands — a risk that Mr. Kanyungu found utterly reckless.

That night, Mr. Kalindera deteriorated sharply. He vomited, suffered diarrhea and begged for water. A nurse tried to insert an IV line, but failed to find a vein. Soon after, he died quietly in his sleep.

Nobody came to collect the body, leaving Mr. Kanyungu to spend the night alongside his dead companion, unable to sleep.

“I don’t want to go back inside,” he said the next morning, sitting outside in the sun. “I’ve seen too many people die.”

A truck arrived to carry Mr. Kalindera’s flower-print coffin to a forest clearing, a few miles outside town, where Ebola victims were being buried.

Over 100 freshly dug graves were squeezed amid a cluster of towering palm trees whose fronds formed a vaulted canopy over the impromptu cemetery. Plain wooden crosses bore no names. Gravediggers leaned on shovels, some swigging from beer bottles. The smell of hashish wafted through the air.

Mr. Sakara’s Red Cross volunteers maneuvered the coffin toward an open pit, struggling to keep their balance in the narrow spaces between graves. One slipped, causing the coffin to lurch, then fall into the grave with a thud. Onlookers grimaced or cried out in shock.

With no priest and no prayers, the gravediggers quickly scooped the rich, loamy earth into the grave. Wailing filled the air. One woman fell to the ground as soil hit Mr. Kalindera’s coffin. “Oh, Moïse!” she cried.

Consolée was absent — family members had forced her into isolation, fearing her visit to the ward might have infected her.

Yards away, another group began digging the next grave. A third group arrived, bearing a coffin for burial.

One mourner turned toward us.

“This is the fault of the white people,” she said loudly. “You brought Ebola here.”

Jeering erupted, led by the gravediggers.

“You killed him! I hope you are happy!”

“Let’s attack them!”

Two men beside us debated whether we were really journalists. Another walked up, holding out a hoe. “Take it, white man,” he said to me. “Help us dig.”

One of the gravediggers waved a toy wooden rifle, then pointed it at me.

As we slipped away, handfuls of soil fell on our heads, thrown from the direction of Mr. Kalindera’s grave.

The next day, Mr. Kanyungu left the Ebola ward, removing his white face mask to reveal a broad smile.

His second test had come back negative.

He was going home.

item.title: Eisenkot Accuses Netanyahu of Fueling ‘Racist’ Hostility Against Arabs
item.description:
Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief who is trying to form the next Israeli government, accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday of fueling a “racist” campaign against the country’s Arab citizens, in some of the strongest public criticism of his rival’s attacks on the community.

The comments were made days after Mr. Netanyahu delivered a divisive speech to the opening session of Parliament, or the Knesset, in which he referred to Arab lawmakers as “terror supporters” and “haters of Israel.” Diplomats and analysts condemned the remarks as a brazen display of hatred and incitement against Arab citizens, who make up about 20 percent of the overall population, and voted in massive numbers in inconclusive elections last month.

“Since the beginning of the election campaign, they have been subjected to a racist and aggressive campaign of delegitimization, fueled by the outgoing prime minister and those around him for political purposes,” Mr. Eisenkot said in a statement on social media.

“Arab citizens of Israel are an integral part of the Israeli story,” he said, adding that it was wrong to malign an entire community.

“The attempt to marginalize them and vilify them collectively is a profound violation of the principles of statesmanship,” Mr. Eisenkot said. “It dishonors Israel’s Declaration of Independence and the values we take pride in as a Jewish and democratic state.”

The Declaration of Independence says all citizens have equal social and political rights “irrespective of religion, race or sex.”

On Sunday, President Isaac Herzog gave Mr. Eisenkot a mandate to try to form a government after 67 of the 120 members of the new Parliament endorsed the opposition leader to become prime minister. He has up to six weeks to create a ruling coalition.

Mr. Netanyahu and his allies have claimed without basis that Arab voters stole the election, after his political bloc won fewer seats than his opponents. The Arab parties have supported Mr. Eisenkot’s effort to form a government and have said they were determined to oust Mr. Netanyahu.

In his speech, Mr. Netanyahu took aim at Arab parties, which received more than 835,000 votes. “To those thinking about establishing a government with those people, I say — are you ready to be dependent on those whose goal is the destruction of the Jewish state?” he said.

The Arab parties that won enough votes to enter the Knesset are Raam, a pragmatic Islamist party, and the Joint List, an alliance of three factions that includes leftists and Palestinian nationalists.

Raam has sought to gain wider acceptance by focusing on issues affecting the Arab citizens of Israel, like violent crime and discriminatory housing policies, than on the plight of Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank.

The Joint List has also fought for the rights of Arab citizens of Israel, but it has frequently criticized Israel’s treatment of Palestinians and has called itself “a genuine democratic alternative to the racist Zionist consensus.”

Mansour Abbas, the chairman of Raam, has condemned the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel as “saddening, heartbreaking,” while officials in the Joint List have denounced the killing of civilians on that day. Both have refused to call Hamas a terrorist group — a condition that Mr. Eisenkot has said parties wishing to join a government under his leadership should accept.

Nadav Eyal, a leading columnist for Yedioth Ahronoth, a centrist Israeli newspaper, said Mr. Eisenkot’s statement pushed back against Mr. Netanyahu’s efforts to delegitimize any cooperation with Arab parties.

Mr. Eisenkot was also sending a more direct message to Arab voters, Mr. Eyal said. “He’s telling them, ‘I see you and I see what they’re trying to do you and your representatives.’”

Still, Mr. Eyal said Mr. Eisenkot’s comments did not suggest that he intended to form a government relying on Arab parties, especially when “they have trouble saying Hamas is a terrorist organization.”

item.title: Two Celebrity Cases Put a Spotlight on British Courts’ Gag Orders
item.description:
Two recent cases have brought new attention to the ways that British laws can allow the wealthy and powerful to silence their critics.

The first was the rape and sexual assault trial of the comedian Russell Brand. Before his conviction last week, Mr. Brand had obtained an injunction prohibiting another accuser from telling almost anyone — including the police, her family and most doctors — about her claims that he assaulted her. (Mr. Brand has denied her allegations.) That injunction, first revealed by Dan Neidle, a tax lawyer and free-expression activist, apparently remains in force.

In the second instance, two British news organizations were temporarily blocked from reporting allegations of sexual misconduct against David Walliams, a television personality and author of children’s books, before a judge declined to make the injunction permanent. The Guardian newspaper and ITV News, a British broadcaster, published investigations last week into the allegations, which Mr. Walliams denies.

Though both men now face public scrutiny, the revelations of how they used court injunctions — essentially gag orders — to protect their reputations have provoked no shortage of public and political outrage. Judges in other cases have issued “super injunctions,” which prohibit publishing any information even about the injunction itself.

“What will the government do to prevent these abuses of process, and stop the abusive injunctions and super injunctions which stop scrutiny, accountability and the work of the free press?” Nick Timothy, the shadow justice minister, asked in Parliament on Tuesday.

The British government is now “looking at what we can do,” Alex Davies-Jones, the government minister responsible for victims of crime and violence against women and girls, said in response.

The government is “determined to do all we can to ensure that anyone who is a perpetrator of these crimes is held to the full force of the law,” Ms. Davies-Jones said.

It’s a long way from the modern media environment to British libel law’s historical roots.

The laws were developed in the 17th century to stop aristocrats from settling their reputational disputes by dueling, Geoffrey Robertson, a London-based human rights lawyer, wrote in the 2023 book “Lawfare.”

In order to make the courts an attractive substitute for combat, civil libel law effectively put the burden of proof on the person alleged to have made an offending statement, rather than the person who brought the suit.

The effort worked; dueling has fallen firmly out of favor. But putting the burden of proof on defendants continues to protect the wealthy and powerful today, Mr. Robertson writes.

In the United States, the burden is reversed. Libel plaintiffs, not defendants, must prove that the statements in question are false. Public figures face an even higher standard: They must show that defamatory statements were made with “actual malice,” meaning that the publisher either knew they were false or had reckless disregard for the truth.

That, along with other First Amendment protections, has created a freer publishing environment in the United States than in the United Kingdom.

As media profits have fallen, it has become even more difficult for British newspapers and television journalists to afford to take on deep-pocketed individuals.

Although media outlets do sometimes decide that publishing is worth the costs, in many cases they simply cannot afford to do so.

Most notoriously, The Sunday Mirror in 1994 chose not to report that Jimmy Savile, a prominent TV personality, had sexually abused children. Although journalists had collected substantial evidence of the abuse, the newspaper’s lawyers reportedly said that the story wasn’t worth the risks of publication.

The police eventually concluded that Mr. Savile had committed hundreds of crimes, including raping 28 children.

Over time, British laws have been used not merely to respond to defamation, but to actively try to prevent speech that could cause distress, said Mark Stephens, a prominent British media lawyer.

This, too, is a significant difference from the United States, where “prior restraint” of speech is particularly disfavored under First Amendment law. In Britain, by contrast, injunctions have been an available tool.

It is difficult to gauge how widely used they are, because they are by nature devised to prevent publicity. Ordinary people can, in principle, avail themselves of those protections, too. But the wealthy and powerful have both more incentive to protect their reputations against negative publicity, and more means to hire lawyers to fight what can be expensive cases. Specialized law firms have made that kind of litigation into a lucrative practice.

“The problem is that we still imagine censorship as a man from the government arriving with a blue pencil and deleting sentences, but modern restrictions are so much more subtle,” Mr. Stephens said.

Mr. Brand’s court order silencing his accuser, for example, was nominally an anti-harassment injunction. Jemima Goldsmith, a former girlfriend of Mr. Brand, wrote this week that she had joined him in requesting the injunction because the accuser had subjected her to vicious, antisemitic threats.

Ms. Goldsmith has also accused Mr. Brand of abusing her during their relationship. Rosamund Unwin, the British journalist whose 2023 reporting revealed Mr. Brand’s sexual misconduct, called her “brave” for speaking out about the abuse and said Ms. Goldsmith had assisted her with her reporting.

The accuser, still under the injunction, has not responded to Ms. Goldsmith. But the order went far beyond just barring harassment, prohibiting the woman from speaking about her assault allegations to anyone, even in private conversations. (The police had previously opened an investigation into the allegations, but closed it without pursuing charges.)

Mr. Walliams, after obtaining a temporary injunction against the news outlets, then tried to secure a permanent one, arguing that publishing the allegations against him might lead him to kill himself.

Citing the public interest in journalism that reveals abuses of power, the court rejected Mr. Walliams’ request for a permanent injunction after finding that the state had already provided measures to protect his life by offering him inpatient psychiatric treatment.

Defenders of the current system argue that injunctions and other tools are needed to safeguard privacy and prevent harassment — both serious considerations that are protected under British law.

“If things are private, they shouldn’t become public unless there’s public interest in doing so,” Hugh Tomlinson, a lawyer known for winning injunctions on behalf of high-profile clients, told the Guardian in 2011. Judges, he said, were best placed to make such decisions.

But Mr. Stephens and others say that overzealous efforts to protect those interests can have other, more damaging effects.

“I think there’s been a move from dealing with the consequences, which is a perfectly legitimate place for the law to be, to trying to prevent the consequences,” Mr. Stephens said. “And when you anticipate the consequences you are always overbroad in your restrictions.”

One meaningful change would be to limit the duration of gag orders so that they automatically expire unless renewed by a court, Mr. Stephens said.

The government could also pass legislation prohibiting orders that prevent people from speaking out about harassment or abuse, as it did last year for employer nondisclosure agreements.

But Mr. Robertson argues for a broader prohibition on injunctions against publishing or revealing information, unless plaintiffs can show that there is “no significant public interest” in the information they are trying to suppress.

“This simple amendment should protect serious journalism,” he writes. “In a MeToo era it must be recognized that there is a public interest in allowing women who have been abused by powerful men to tell their story.”

item.title: Venezuelans Saw Oil as Their Birthright. Now Trump Is Claiming It.
item.description:
Like generations before him, Leonardo Silva grew up steeped in beliefs about the extraordinarily abundant resource that made Venezuela special. All the oil under their feet was theirs, they felt. Virtually free gasoline was a birthright. To be born atop this bounty was like winning the lottery.

Mr. Silva, 38, said his generation viewed oil as a cornerstone of the country’s national identity, when a booming economy allowed Venezuela to occupy a privileged tier in the global order. His children, he said, have a far less rosy view.

“To them oil isn’t important, it’s secondary,” said Mr. Silva, who works at a foundation in Caracas helping people with disabilities. “They don’t have that culture of us being a rich country. They just know that if you don’t work, you don’t eat.”

Oil has shaped Venezuela to an extent that is rare outside the Middle East for more than a century, becoming a defining feature of the social fabric like baseball, beauty pageants or the veneration of the liberation hero Simón Bolívar.

But now the U.S. government is taking control of a huge portion of Venezuela’s oil. And, pressed by economic need, long-held nationalist convictions about oil, starting with the need for sovereign control, are giving way to a more complex web of perspectives.

The ways in which Venezuelans are re-evaluating oil, and by extension their reliance on it, are the result of immense upheaval over the last decade. Oil production plummeted because of mismanagement, political purges, corruption and sanctions.

The cratering of an economy overwhelmingly dependent on oil led to a financial crash marked by widespread deprivation and the exodus of millions of Venezuelans up and down the Americas.

The Trump administration then toppled Venezuela’s leader at the start of the year, took control of oil exports and went even further, forming a partnership with a scandal-plagued Venezuelan oil magnate that would enable the U.S. government to control a huge portion of Venezuela’s reserves.

Delcy Rodríguez, the interim president, has expressed full-throated support for the plan, a sweeping shift for a leader steeped in Chavismo, the political movement that made uncontested dominance over oil one of its tenets.

Ms. Rodríguez has little wriggle room with the Trump administration essentially dictating how she can operate. At the same time, some Venezuelans are so desperate for the economy to improve that they say ceding control over the oil industry is a small price to pay.

“Closing these deals is super urgent,” said María Ines Figueroa, 56, referring to the Trump administration’s takeover of Venezuelan oil reserves as well as other U.S. ventures under consideration.

Ms. Figueroa, a retired public-school teacher in Caracas, said inflation had eroded her pension before the U.S. deposed Venezuela’s last president to less than $1 a month. She now teaches at a private school where she earns $120 a month.

Her hope, she said, was that a revival of the oil industry would create a trickle down that reached into households like her own. “I’m no expert, but I think this could work,” Ms. Figueroa said.

Other Venezuelans are openly welcoming U.S. dominance over Venezuela’s oil, reflecting how opposing voices, including on the right, are becoming more bold after three decades of leftist rule marked by economic devastation and repression of dissent.

“I don’t care about the oil,” Maria Elisa Smith, a right-wing polemicist known for her racist vitriol, said recently on social media. “Oil never gave me anything good, just a miserable, socialist country.”

Still, sharp indignation bubbled up after President Trump announced the deal in August that gave the United States access to 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil, then repeatedly boasted about it.

Many across the ideological spectrum were angry, from opposition leaders to prominent figures of Chavismo, the movement that has controlled Venezuelan politics for three decades.

Luis Britto García, a playwright who has written widely about oil’s importance in Venezuela, said Trump’s deal laid bare the “unlimited pillage” Venezuela was experiencing as the Trump administration exerted tight financial control over oil revenues.

Long before Venezuela’s economy crashed, oil had ceased to be merely a geological resource or an export statistic, evolving into a prism through which Venezuelans contemplated their own society or compared it to others.

Some credited oil for creating modern Venezuela: Its reserves rank among the world’s largest, and since the first gushers were found, oil gave Venezuela an income neighboring countries envied.

Others saw oil as cursing Venezuela with corruption, dependency and dysfunction, citing how authoritarian and democratic leaders alike wielded the revenues to advance their own ambitions at the nation’s expense.

For decades until Venezuela’s economy collapsed, motorists viewed practically free gasoline as an entitlement, spawning a car culture of 1970s-style gas hogs and fuel-devouring SUV’s that can make the oversized vehicles filling Texas’s roads seem quaint.

Even today, oil permeates everything from rap lyrics to the memes Venezuelans share on their phones. Writers have wrestled with Venezuela’s entanglement with oil so much that there’s an entire literary tradition devoted to it.

Oil even shapes the Spanish that Venezuelans speak: “Este hombre trabaja más que un balancín,” is just one popular expression, a nod to an industry once considered a steppingstone to a better life.

It can be translated as “This man works more than a pump jack,” referring to the iconic machinery functioning nonstop to pull crude oil from subterranean wells.

Cósimo Mandrillo, the director of Monte Ávila, a state-owned publishing house, said that despite shifting political winds as the United States takes greater control of the country’s resources, Venezuelans maintain a connection to oil so intimate that it “borders on the subconscious.”

“Oil penetrates every fiber of national life,” Mr. Mandrillo said. “It is so deeply absorbed in the collective psyche that we navigate its presence almost by instinct.”

Hugo Chávez, who ruled Venezuela from 1999 until his death in 2013, seized on this visceral connection like few rulers before him. Constantly clashing with the United States, he made state control over oil the centerpiece of his socialist-inspired Bolivarian revolution.

At home, he used oil revenues to ease poverty and consolidate power. Projecting power abroad, Mr. Chávez propped up Cuba, built international coalitions to defy U.S. influence and launched Telesur, a pan-Latin American television network.

Nicolás Maduro, Mr. Chávez’s successor, doubled down on the approach. Even as the economy unraveled, he framed oil not as a commodity on a balance sheet but as the fuel for consolidating his authoritarian rule.

In a bid to circumvent U.S. sanctions, Mr. Maduro launched his own cryptocurrency called the Petro, claiming each token was backed by a barrel of oil. But the crypto scheme collapsed in connection to a corruption scandal at the national oil company.

Even before Mr. Maduro was overthrown by U.S. forces in January, the ways in which Venezuelans viewed oil had begun to change, largely because of economic desperation after production plunged.

It was not until 2020, under the cover of acute fuel shortages and the Covid-19 pandemic, that Mr. Maduro effectively ended the era of universal, nearly free gasoline, introducing a dollarized rate at most gas stations.

Until then, Chavismo had recast the Caracazo, the massive riots in 1989 sparked by a jump in fuel prices, as one of its spiritual catalysts. As a result, highly subsidized gasoline became an untouchable third rail of Venezuelan politics.

Standard gasoline in Venezuela for most motorists costs about $1.89 a gallon (still far less than the prevailing prices in the United States and many other nations), alongside a tightly restricted, subsidized and cheaper tier linked to a social rationing program.

In an energy-rich country where electricity shortages are a part of life in many cities, such rationing routinely produces the surreal sight of long lines of motorists waiting to fill up.

The dysfunction plaguing much of the economy comes as Mr. Trump is unsparingly direct about using his chokehold on Venezuela’s government to extract one deal after another.

As Venezuela emerges as essentially a vassal state of a pre-eminent superpower, Margarita López Maya, a historian, said it was not surprising some Venezuelans were prepared to accept U.S. control over the country’s oil, if only because they saw no other option.

“Chavismo,” she said, “has reduced us to a state of global humiliation, kneeling before the United States.”

item.title: Ukraine’s Starshield Access Is Being Restricted Again, Zelensky Says
item.description:
Ukrainian military operations were disrupted again this week along the front lines because of restrictions on Starshield, the satellite internet system developed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX and controlled by the U.S. government, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Friday.

Mr. Zelensky told reporters that speed limits of about 100 miles per hour were being enforced for Ukrainian devices connected to the system. It would be the second time in recent weeks that Ukraine’s Starshield connectivity had been throttled. The previous restrictions caused Ukrainian drones to lose their connection to the system if they flew above certain speeds.

Mr. Zelensky said that the latest speed limits took effect on Monday and were being enforced over Russian-occupied territories, not over all of Ukraine. That hurts Ukraine’s ability to strike Russian troops with drones in those territories.

Imposing restrictions on occupied territories is “very dangerous, because it already has political implications,” Mr. Zelensky said. “If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognizing the temporarily occupied territories as not ours,” he added.

Mr. Zelensky said separately in his nightly speech that the Starshield limits hurt Ukraine’s ability to use newly developed interceptors to protect its cities from Russia’s jet-powered drones. It is likely, however, that those limits would not affect interceptors in Kyiv, the capital, which is being battered by jet-powered drones but is far from the front lines.

Mr. Musk and SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment on Friday evening. SpaceX had earlier told Axios that the Ukrainian claim about throttled connectivity was false.

The U.S. Defense Department said on Friday that it was looking into the matter. It did not immediately respond to questions on Saturday about its potential role in the slowdown.

Limits on Starshield were first imposed in all of Ukraine for about 10 days in October as President Trump and his administration were pressuring its leaders to stop attacking Russian oil refineries, hoping to lower diesel prices before the U.S. midterm elections.

At the time, Ukrainian officials expressed fears that the limits were meant to force Kyiv to capitulate to Moscow. The changes, which caused drones to fall from the skies on the front line, still have not been fully explained.

Got a confidential news tip? The New York Times would like to hear from readers who want to share messages and materials with our journalists.

Starshield is the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink, which is also used by the Ukrainian military. Ukraine uses Starlink for communication, while it uses Starshield for certain kinds of air defense and to guide drones in Russian-occupied territory.

Last month, SpaceX said in a letter to Congress about the previous disruptions that no changes had been made to Starshield because it was under the control of the U.S. government. But changes were made to Starlink, the company said, because Ukraine had violated the system’s terms of service by using it for “offensive military aviation missions.”

On Friday, Mr. Zelensky did not mention any renewed limits on Starlink, and Ukrainian officials this week only referred to restrictions on Starshield.

Serhiy Beskrestnov, a Ukrainian military expert who advises Mr. Zelensky on weapons technologies, wrote on social media on Thursday that “the operating speed of Starshield while in motion has been restricted again.”

“Our relief didn’t last long,” he added.

Mr. Beskrestnov said the Ukrainian military was once again having communication problems with its helicopters that pursue drones targeting cities, and with the jet-powered interceptors used to shoot down Russia’s jet-powered drones.

The Ukrainian claims of another Starshield slowdown came shortly after the latest round of trilateral peace talks between officials from the United States, Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates. It was the first time since February that Russian and Ukrainian representatives had met in person.

Mr. Zelensky also told reporters on Friday that Ukraine planned to ask Congress for more U.S. weapons and for additional sanctions against Russia.

He said that “if Ukraine can move in this direction, and the U.S. Congress can consider supporting such an idea, then by the end of the year the parties really have an opportunity to try to reach an agreement on at least some de-escalation.”

Such a package would likely have to wait until the newly elected Congress, which will be fully controlled by Democrats, takes office in January. Republicans in Congress have largely bowed to Mr. Trump’s desire to lower military support for Ukraine.

Andrew E. Kramer, Oleksandra Mykolyshyn, Dzvinka Pinchuk, Eric Schmitt and Ryan Mac contributed reporting.

item.title: ‘Get Focused on London’: How Iran’s Agents Attacked European Targets
item.description:
As the U.S.-Israel war in Iran raged earlier this year, a man linked to Iranian criminal networks perched in front of a computer, on a video call with a teenager in London. The man wanted to make sure the teen, who was moments away from setting fire to a synagogue, carried out his plans.

“Light it up like a Christman tree,” the man, an Iraqi named Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, urged the 17-year-old, according to U.S. prosecutors. The teen climbed over a wall and tossed a bomb through a broken window. “J’s mic is muted,” read the text on Mr. al-Hassani’s computer screen.

The synagogue arson in April was a small, violent part of Iran’s efforts to force an end to the bombing campaign that was pummeling the country, according to American investigators.

The attack was described in a federal indictment filed in New York this week. It revealed extensive new details about a wave of violence against Jewish institutions in Europe and U.S. targets, including a British air base used by American bombers. Prosecutors hold Iran’s agents responsible for the assaults.

Within days of the war starting, Mr. al-Hassani and at least two associates, including an operative for Iran’s powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, began plotting the attacks in Europe, prosecutors said. The men talked about procuring drones and missiles from contacts in Iran. They pored over a map of London, with one saying they should “get focused” on targeting the British capital. Soon after, attacks hit temples and other Jewish sites in London.

In the fight against much stronger conventional forces, Iran has found ways to impose costs on its adversaries without inviting a full military response. One major aspect of Iran’s strategy is its embrace of small-time criminals to conduct low-cost assaults against vulnerable targets that are part of everyday life.

Since the U.S.-Israeli war began, Iran and its proxies — who sometimes act on their own — have stepped up such attacks, particularly in Britain, which has allowed the United States to use its military bases to strike Iranian forces. By hitting American allies, Iran aims to sow fear and try to weaken their support for the U.S. and Israeli military deployments, experts said.

“What we are seeing right now is the application of a playbook Iran has refined over decades,” said Adrian Shtuni, an associate fellow with the International Center for Counter-Terrorism. In addition to the criminal attacks, he also cited Iran’s efforts to build proxy militant networks outside Iran and enhance its abilities to carry out cyberattacks.

The threat persists. This week, as many as a dozen U.S. military aircraft based at R.A.F. Mildenhall in England were evacuated to other bases in Europe, including in Germany, after intelligence officials detected an Iran-backed drone plot against the base, three American officials said.

The Mildenhall air base, about 70 miles northeast of London in Suffolk, is a major hub for U.S. Air Force operations in Europe. It has a large air refueling wing and a Special Operations wing, with about 1,000 military personnel there.

The officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss operational matters, said analysts had received a general warning, but commanders were not taking chances. Mohsen Rezaei, Iran’s national security adviser, threatened in an interview on Lebanese television this week to hit U.S. bases in Europe if they are used for attacks against his country.

At the center of Iran’s operations this year in Europe, prosecutors said, is an Iraqi sitting in a Brooklyn jail named Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi. He is a high-ranking commander in Kataib Hezbollah, one of Iran’s most powerful proxies in Iraq. He was captured in Turkey and charged in May with carrying out attacks in Europe and plotting to attack Jewish sites in the United States.

Prosecutors said he also has close ties to the I.R.G.C., the long arm of Iran’s terrorist apparatus.

Mr. al Saadi implored two associates to help him target Europe, investigators said. The I.R.G.C. operative, Mohsen Mohajeri, is an Iranian national. The other, Mr. al-Hassani, is known as “Ali” and has extensive criminal ties according to American court documents.

Days into the war, Mr. al-Saadi and Mr. Mohajeri began conspiring, prosecutors said. It was Mr. Mohajeri who mentioned acquiring drones and missiles from contacts in Iran. He sent Mr. al-Saadi a bank account number to buy “equipment for jihad.”

He said he would join Mr. al-Saadi so they could direct the attacks together in Iraq, pledging, “I will not return to Iran until we take revenge.” Mr. Mohajeri traveled to Iraq a couple of days later, and the attacks began in Europe shortly after.

Seven were in Britain, the most of any country. “We need to get focused on London,” Mr. Mohajeri told Mr. al-Hassani in early April while they studied a map of the city on a laptop, according to prosecutors.

Mr. al-Hassani, investigators said, had previously lived in the United Kingdom and had contacts there whom he tapped to carry out attacks.

In an April 15 arson attempt on a synagogue in the London neighborhood of Finchley, investigators said, Mr. al-Hassani spoke over video with a mask-wearing perpetrator. “Go as close as the gate as you can,” he said.

On April 17, all three men were in a room together and on a FaceTime video call with an assailant while he attacked a Jewish charity organization. While the call was projected onto a large screen, Mr. al-Hassani coached the perpetrator to light an incendiary device.

“Light one in your hand,” he said.

“Light it.”

“Throw the fourth one.”

While he directed the attack, Mr. Al-Saadi recorded it. Mr. Mohajeri filmed them both.

The men were behind a new group calling itself HAYI that claimed responsibility for at least six terrorist attacks in and around London, according to court filings. Perhaps the most notorious was the burning of four ambulances belonging to a Jewish volunteer service in Golders Green, a heavily Jewish neighborhood.

In the teenager’s synagogue arson attack in late April, nobody was injured, and the damage was minor. The teen later pleaded guilty and said he did not know it was a temple and that he did not hate Jews.

HAYI has claimed responsibility for about 18 attacks or plots across Europe and the United States in the spring. Mr. al-Saadi also directed blasts against U.S. bank branches in Amsterdam and Paris before he was arrested in May.

As he sat in a jail cell in Brooklyn, Mr. al-Saadi apparently had contingency plans. In conversations with his family in Iraq over the summer, he passed coded messages intended for his two associates, prosecutors said.

In late July, Mr. al-Saadi asked his sister, “What are they doing about all our old work?” and she replied that it was ongoing.

By August, according to investigators, Mr. al-Hassani was paying accomplices in Britain to initiate an attack on R.A.F. Fairford, the air base that hosted American bombers that flew sorties to Iran. The men — at least five of them — secured vans and barrels of fuel. They researched chemical accelerants and metallic objects that could be used as shrapnel.

Mr. al-Hassani took care to make sure they did the job correctly. He told the men to place custom-made decals on the three vans so they looked like they were part of fuel delivery and swimming pool supply businesses.

They waited for the green light. Investigators say Mr. al-Saadi gave it on Sept. 24, again through his family.

A couple of nights later, Mr. al-Hassani directed the men to drive to the base, talking with them during their journey. But the authorities had been aware of a vague threat to the base. At least two of the vans encountered a security roadblock, blocking the route that Mr. al-Hassani was instructing them to take.

Early in the morning of Sept. 27, the police apprehended the five men and recovered the vans. They never penetrated the base.

But the close call highlighted vulnerabilities in Europe’s security and played into Iran’s effort to raise the cost of Western support for the U.S.-Israeli war.

“They are playing the long game,” Mr. Shtuni said of Iran, “the only one they can.”

Eric Schmitt contributed reporting from Washington.

item.title: A ‘Generational Clash’ Is Fueling Europe’s Protests
item.description:
Sébastien Ducros, a French data analyst who supports the widespread student protests in his country, has identified an obvious culprit for the lack of government funds for dilapidated schools.

“A huge portion of the money is going toward retirees, while many other things are being neglected,” said Mr. Ducros, 36. “I honestly think — even if it feels strange to say — that people like my parents are in a position where they should and could” surrender some of their pension payments, he added, saying that they were about to retire.

But Laurent Grinwald, 72, who retired recently after decades as a postal worker, isn’t eager for his pension to be reduced, particularly to pay for other state-funded services. Especially, he said, as rents and the cost of living have shot up.

“We’ve been working all this time,” Mr. Grinwald said, “and now, suddenly, the stance is, ‘Well, no, we’re going to start taking a bit more?’”

This disagreement embodies a broader question for Europe, one that is at the heart of mass antigovernment demonstrations planned for Saturday in France, as well as recent protests driven by frustrated young people in countries including Belgium, Germany, Greece, Italy and Portugal. As Europeans live longer, should the needs of the young be eclipsed by their parents’ and grandparents’ pensions, routinely the largest items in Europe’s national budgets?

“It’s a generational clash,” said Jorge Galindo, the director of EsadeEcPol, an independent think tank in Spain, which has some of the most generous pensions in Europe.

In much of Europe, spending on a growing population of older people has come at the expense of services and subsidies for young workers whose tax contributions help to fund pensions.

Spiraling defense costs, prompted by American pressure and Russian aggression, have also made it harder for governments to balance their books. And high interest rates have driven up the costs of servicing state debt.

All of that, coupled with rising rents and house prices, has compounded a sense of generational injustice among young people. Only 38 percent of people aged 15 to 30 think that policymakers consider the long-term consequences of their decisions, according to a recent European Union survey. Only a third believe that today’s young people have the same shot at success as young people 30 years ago did, the survey also found.

The enormous financial burden of pensions — they gobble up around 40 percent of the spending on social protections in the European Union — has not been lost on European governments.

Over the past decade, many countries have tried to tinker with pension formulas, trying to cut costs while postponing major political blowback. To many older Europeans, pensions are considered the sacrosanct base of the European welfare system.

Often, they have avoided cutting what each retiree is paid while gradually raising the age at which citizens qualify for those payments — to 67 from 65, for example, or older. Denmark plans to raise it to 70 by 2040.

Even that approach has had a political cost. When President Emmanuel Macron of France tried in 2023 to raise France’s retirement age to 64 from 62, it prompted such furious protests that the government eventually froze the measure. But that gave the country a different problem.

With one of the highest debt levels in Europe, France says it cannot afford to spend more on education — which has prompted the youth anger spurring the wave of unrest.

Other countries have tried other ways of softening the generational competition. Britain plans to save billions by slowing the speed at which its pension payments increase over time, while Spain has enlarged its pool of taxpaying workers.

Spain chose in 2011 to raise its pension age to 67 in most cases. Then the current left-wing government enlarged the pension bill by ensuring that pension payments would grow in line with inflation, protecting recipients from rising prices but putting an enormous strain on the budget.

To offset those costs, it has bucked the European trend and opened its doors to immigrant labor — more than 1.7 million foreigners have entered the Spanish work force since 2018.

Those workers have increased tax revenue, which in turn helps to fund pension contributions, but eventually, experts note, they will age, too.

Spain will spend 17.3 percent of its gross domestic product in 2050 on pensions, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development — roughly four percentage points higher than now. That means the government would then be spending the equivalent in today’s terms of an additional $67 billion every year on pensions. It currently spends roughly $79 billion on education.

Despite the competition for resources, many of the young people protesting throughout Europe are loath to blame their elders.

“Honestly,” said Alice Cossa, 22, an Italian student who protested recently in Venice, “we’ve never talked about it.”

Left-wing demonstrators often say that pensions and other benefits can be funded by taxing the rich and corporations. Their right-wing counterparts suggest cutting immigration, blaming immigrants for soaking up welfare benefits.

Some feel, though, that at least some pensions, namely those received by wealthy older people, should be reassessed.

“We young people have less and less and less,” said Alejandro Rojano, 28, a bank employee who lives in a basement apartment in Madrid with a roommate. He said even his own nonagenarian grandparents received “way” more than his monthly salary, which was less than 2,000 euros, or less than $2,200. No political party would dare cut the benefits of such a dependable and powerful voting bloc as retirees, he lamented, adding of the pension payouts, “It makes no sense, you know?”

Mr. Galindo, the think tank director, said that given the entrenched political interests in protecting retirees, young people might need to form an essentially single-issue voting bloc. Because European governments are typically formed from coalitions of smaller parties, such a party could become pivotal and have its concerns taken seriously with only a handful of seats.

But young people are a shrinking demographic in Europe, and the number of older people, who are more likely to exercise political power through union and party memberships, is booming.

And young and middle-aged Europeans are reluctant to cut a benefit that they hope to enjoy in the future.

As Daniel Ramo, 46, left a recent teachers’ strike in Madrid protesting dismal salaries and packed classrooms, he said that he personally looked forward to receiving his generous Spanish pension after making €2,100 a month after taxes. In the meantime, the benefits of his parents’ pensions would trickle down to help him through tough times.

“I’m on strike knowing I’ll have to borrow money from my father,” said Mr. Ramo, who said his father’s pension made him the top earner in the family.

From the perspective of retirees, the hard-earned benefit helps keep families, and European society, going.

“We personally make more than our children do,” said Encarna Matilla, 72, as she took a walk in sunny Retiro Park in Madrid. She said her 88-year-old husband, who worked from 14 to 70, received a pension payment of €2,700, 60 percent higher than Spain’s median salary, and helped support her great-grandchildren.

“We are the safety net,” she said.

Ségolène Le Stradic contributed reporting from Paris, Josephine de La Bruyère from Rome and Carlos Barragán from Madrid.
